Commentary on the Song of Songs by the blessed Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus. Theodoret to the most God-beloved Bishop John.

To interpret the divine oracles one needs a soul that has been cleansed and freed from every stain. One also needs a mind that has wings, can see into divine things and is bold enough to enter the inner sanctuary of the Spirit. And one needs a tongue that serves the mind and expresses its contemplation worthily. My soul, however, is crusted over with a great heap of sins. My mind is drowned in the cares of the affairs entrusted to me, and is therefore lowly and earthbound, unable to look closely into the divine oracles. Besides this, my tongue is even more sluggish and slow than my mind. But you, my dear friend, have commanded me to interpret the book of the Song of Songs and to set out plainly and clearly the meaning of what it says in riddles and mysteries. So I have dared what is beyond my strength, though I am caught up in countless cares of town and country, military and civil, ecclesiastical and public. I have faced the depth of the sea and dared to go down into the depth of the text, in order to bring up for you the pearl of its meaning. I have not taken oil into my mouth, as divers do, to use a man-made light to help me search for what I seek,

but prayer and supplication, which those who long to reach the meaning of the divine oracles need above all else. For the blessed David taught us to say, "Unveil my eyes, and I will perceive wondrous things out of your law." Since we have been taught this, let us implore divine grace to show us the meaning of this book.

Some people slander the Song of Songs. They do not believe the book is spiritual, and they weave tales that not even silly old women would babble. They dare to say that the wise Solomon wrote it about himself and Pharaoh's daughter. Others of the same company have invented the idea that the bride is Abishag the Shunammite instead of Pharaoh's daughter. Those who have thought more decently than these have called the work a royal discourse, naming the people the bride and the king the bridegroom. Therefore, as I begin this commentary, I have thought it necessary first to refute this false and harmful interpretation, and then to set out clearly the purpose of the text.

These people ought to have realized that the blessed Fathers are far wiser and more spiritual than they are. It was the Fathers who placed this book among the divine Scriptures, accepted it into the canon as spiritual and declared it fit for the Church. Had they thought otherwise, they would never have counted among the holy Scriptures a book whose subject was incontinence and love of pleasure. But why should I speak of the Fathers here below, when I can call on the testimony of the divine Spirit himself? Some of the divine Scriptures were burned by Manasseh, who outdid in wickedness and impiety all who came before and after him. Others vanished entirely at the time of the captivity, when the Babylonians burned the divine temple, laid waste the city and enslaved the people. After many years, when the people had been called back, the blessed Ezra, a man outstanding in virtue and filled with the all-holy Spirit, as the facts proclaim, wrote out again the Scriptures that we need and that bring salvation. He wrote out not only the writings of Moses but also the history of Joshua, of the Judges and of the Kings, and the story of the noble Job, and the sacred melody of David, the gladness of the Church, and the sixteen prophets, and the Proverbs of the wise Solomon, and Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. How then, my good sirs, can the book have the meaning you claim? Ezra wrote these things, and he did not write them from copies. He wrote them filled with the divine Spirit, so as to hand down their benefit in writing to all people. For licentious

writings come not from the divine Spirit but from the opposing spirit. For according to the blessed Paul, "the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control." If self-control is the fruit of the divine Spirit, then clearly incontinence is the fruit of its opposite. Yet you say that the book of the Song of Songs has incontinence as its subject. Do you see where this blasphemy leads? Abuse of this book is an outrage against the all-holy Spirit. It was when he was filled with the Spirit's grace that the blessed Ezra renewed the book after it had been destroyed, as I said. Knowing this, the blessed Fathers ranked it among the divine Scriptures.

Many of the ancients also wrote commentaries on it, and those who did not comment on it passage by passage adorned their own writings with quotations from it. Many recognized the book as spiritual. Among them were Eusebius of Palestine, Origen the Egyptian, and Cyprian of Carthage, who also wore the crown of martyrdom, as well as those older than they and nearer to the apostles. So did those who were eminent in the Churches after them: Basil the Great, when he interpreted the beginning of Proverbs; both Gregories, the one boasting of kinship with Basil and the other of friendship; Diodore, the noble champion of true religion; John, who to this day waters the whole world with the streams of his teaching; and, to sum up and avoid making my discourse too long, all who came after them.

Let us consider, then, whether it is right to spurn so many great men, and even to despise the all-holy Spirit himself, in order to follow one's own notions. Such people do not heed the one who said well, "The reasonings of mortals are timid, and their devisings unsure." Nor do they listen to the blessed Paul, who says of certain people that "they became futile in their reasonings, and their senseless heart was darkened." Therefore we cry out with the blessed Peter, "We must obey God rather than men." And we will say to them as well: "Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge. For we cannot help speaking of what we have seen and heard through the Spirit."

But we should not care only for ourselves and ignore the harm done to them. So come, let us ask what gave rise to their error, and let us offer them whatever cure we can from the divine Scriptures. I suppose that when they read this work, they see in it perfumes and kisses, thighs and belly and navel, cheeks and eyes, lilies and apples, nard, myrrh-oil and myrrh, and other such things. Because they do not know the idioms of divine Scripture, they would not go beneath the surface, pass beyond the veil of the letter, enter in by the Spirit, and with unveiled face behold the glory of the Lord as in a mirror.

Instead they understood these words in a carnal sense and ran aground on that blasphemy. They ought to have realized that in the Old Testament too divine Scripture says many things figuratively, using some names to signify other things.

For example, when it speaks of the Babylonian king, it gives neither his proper name nor the general name for his nature. It does not call him Nebuchadnezzar, nor does it call him a man. Instead it says: "The great eagle with great wings, long in span, full of talons, who has the leading to enter Lebanon; and he took the choice parts of the cedar and cropped off its tender tips." No one has ever taken the eagle to be an eagle, or Lebanon to be Lebanon, or the cedar to be a cedar. The eagle is the king, since the eagle is a royal creature. He has great wings because his kingdom is broad, and he is full of talons because his army is huge. Scripture says he has "the leading" because he did what he did under the guidance of the divine will. It calls Jerusalem "Lebanon" because of its dense, thick growth of spiritual gifts. The tender parts of the cedar are those who were well fed, devoted to luxury and eminent in rank. Understanding the text in this way is customary not only for those raised in true religion but even for Jews, who understand the divine Scriptures more grossly and carnally.

The blessed Zechariah also says: "Open your doors, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars; let the pine wail, for the cedar has fallen." Here too we do not take Lebanon to be Lebanon, or cedars to be cedars, or fire to be fire, or pines to be pines. The fire is again the Babylonian, whom Ezekiel called an eagle. Lebanon is Jerusalem. The cedars are those laden with wealth and splendid in rank, and the pines are those of lower standing. Hence he adds, "Let the pine wail, for the cedar has fallen," because the great suffered greatly.

But why should I list everything that divine Scripture says figuratively? Let us leave the rest aside and show that in the Old Testament too the God of all speaks to the multitude of the Jews as to a woman. He uses the same kinds of names for parts of the body that Solomon used when he wrote about this bride. Thus the God of all says to Ezekiel: "Son of man, testify to Jerusalem about her iniquities, and say: Thus says Adonai the Lord to Jerusalem: Your root and your birth are from the land of Canaan. Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite. As for your birth, on the day you were born your navel was not cut, and they did not bind your breasts, and you were not washed in water

for salvation, nor were you rubbed with salt, nor were you wrapped in swaddling cloths. No eye pitied you enough to do even one of these things for you, or felt anything for you. You were cast out on the open field because of the crookedness of your soul on the day you were born. And I passed by you and saw you weltering in your blood. And I said to you: From your blood, life; multiply. I have made you like the sprouts of the field. And you multiplied and grew great and entered into cities of cities. Your breasts were set upright and your hair sprang up. But you were naked and shameful. And I passed by you and saw you, and behold, it was your time, the time of those who lodge together. And I spread my wings over you and covered your shame. And I swore to you and entered into a covenant with you, says Adonai the Lord, and you became mine. And I washed you with water and washed your blood from you, and anointed you with oil. I clothed you in embroidered garments and shod you with blue leather, girded you with fine linen and put a veil of fine hair-work around you. I adorned you with ornaments: I put bracelets on your arms and a necklace around your neck. I gave you a ring for your nose and earrings for your ears, and a crown of boasting for your head." And a little later: "You ate fine flour and honey and oil, and you became exceedingly beautiful, and your fame spread among the nations because of your beauty." And again a little later: "And after all your wickedness, says Adonai the Lord, you built yourself a brothel and set up a display for yourself in every square. At the head of every road you built your brothels. You defiled your beauty and spread your legs for every passer-by and multiplied your harlotry. You played the harlot with the sons of Egypt, your neighbours, the men of great flesh, and many times you played the harlot to provoke me to anger." And again a little later: "You were not like a harlot who gathers her wages. You are like the adulterous wife who, while under her husband, goes after strangers; she takes wages from her husband and gives wages besides to all who play the harlot with her. All harlots are given wages, but you gave wages to all your lovers and loaded them with gifts to come to you from all around for your harlotry. Your harlotry was a perversion unlike that of other women, and none after you will play the harlot so. In giving wages when no wages were given to you, you became perverse." And so on, in the same vein.

What would those who blaspheme the book of the Song of Songs and dare to read it licentiously say when they find such things said in the Old Testament too about the multitude of the Jews?

For look: here too we find breasts, navel, legs, hands, nostrils and ears, beauty, love, embrace and union, and all of them spoken by the God of all. Yet we understand none of it just as we read it, nor do we obey the letter that kills. Instead we go within the letter and search out the mind of the Spirit, and being enlightened by him, we take the things of the Spirit spiritually.

When we hear God say to Jerusalem, "Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite," we understand a kinship not of nature but of disposition. By nature they were descendants of Abraham, who traced his line from Shem. But by the depravity of their conduct they were akin to the race of accursed Canaan. That is why he says that their father was an Amorite and their mother a Hittite, for these were children of Canaan. They had a kinship with those whose wickedness they imitated. That is why the blessed John the Baptist said to those who came out to him: "Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bear fruit worthy of repentance, and do not presume to say to yourselves, We have Abraham as our father." He called those who boasted of Abraham a brood of vipers because of their kinship in wickedness. And when some said to the Lord himself, "We have Abraham as our father," he answered, "You are of your father the devil." Showing the reason, he adds, "and you want to do the works of your father." And showing what those works are, he says, "He was a murderer from the beginning." In the same way the God of all said here, "Your root and your birth are from the land of Canaan; your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite."

Then he describes their life in Egypt, which was neglected and received no care: "On the day you were born," he says, "they did not bind your breasts." He speaks figuratively of both the breasts and their binding, because it is the custom for virgins to take care of their breasts from childhood. That is why God says through the prophet Jeremiah, "Will a bride forget her ornament, or a virgin her breast-band?" Virgins take care of these things because they wish to please their bridegrooms. After the time of its sojourn in Egypt the multitude of the Jews received no care and gave no thought to the parts of virtue. So he rightly says, "On the day you were born they did not bind your breasts." That is, they gave no care to the nourishing part of the soul, which produces nourishing milk, so that in due time it might offer the breasts of teaching to those who came after. Keeping to the same figure, he says, "You were not washed in water." That is: you did not wash off the filth of Egyptian idolatry. Instead,

as though you were born when you came out of that slavery, you still bear the marks of birth. You have not washed them off but are still covered with your mother's filth. Next he adds, "Nor were you rubbed with salt," which midwives customarily apply to newborn babies. This too we shall understand according to the laws of allegory. We know that salt means spiritual understanding and divine teaching, which tightens what is rotting and keeps it sound. That is why the Lord said to the disciples, "Have salt," and again, "You are the salt of the earth." In the Old Testament too we find that no sacrifice was offered without salt.

In the same way we understand "Your navel was not cut." Those skilled in such matters say that the navel is a kind of root of the embryo, since through it, as through a root, the embryo draws its nourishment, grows and is brought to completion. So he rightly says here that Jerusalem's navel had not been cut. She had been born out of Egypt, yet she was still drawing on Egyptian idolatry and taking that evil nourishment from her mother's womb.

"And I passed by you," he says, "and saw you weltering in your blood." By this he means the sacrifices offered to idols. "And I said to you: From your blood, life; multiply." He allowed them to offer sacrifice but decreed that they sacrifice to him. He did not need sacrifice himself, but he came down to the level of their weakness. In effect he says: "You delight in sacrifices and blood. Do not sacrifice to demons, but offer your sacrifices to me. I put up with this, though I need no victims, because I am working for your salvation in every way." That is why he says, "From your blood, life; multiply."

Let us understand "Your breasts were set upright" in the same way. It means: "Before, they sagged because of your great licentiousness and incontinence and your mad passion for idols. But once I cared for them, they were set upright and became, as it were, virginal." He is pointing to the change for the better, the movement toward things above and the acquiring of self-control. "And your hair," he says, "sprang up": that is, you were stripped of every ornament, but suddenly you had hair that could adorn you. "But you were naked and shameful": for the law had not yet been given, nor the tabernacle built, nor the bridal gifts presented. Hence he adds, "And I passed by you and saw you, and behold, it was your time, the time of those who lodge together." In other words: "You had come of age for marriage and were ready for union." "Therefore I spread my wings over you and covered your shame." By the wings he means his various gifts: the priesthood, prophecy, leadership of the people, kingship, the miracles, and those ineffable gifts.

"And I swore to you." This can be found plainly in the writings of the great Moses: "For I will lift up my hand to heaven," he says, "and swear by my right hand, and say: As I live

forever." And again: "But as I live, and as my name lives, the glory of the Lord shall fill all the earth." So he reminds her of the oaths he made to her, saying, "I swore to you and entered into a covenant with you, says Adonai the Lord." In effect he says: "The marriage was lawful. Agreements were made between us, and marriage contracts followed with lawful terms. They stated that if you broke the agreed terms, you would be thrown out of the house, stripped of the bridal gifts, and sent away naked, just as you came in. For you brought nothing to the marriage. But when you were filthy, I cleansed you; when you lacked salt, I seasoned you; when you were naked, I clothed you; and when you were licentious, I made your breasts upright." Hence he adds: "And I entered into a covenant with you, says Adonai the Lord, and you became mine. And I washed you with water and washed your blood from you, and anointed you with oil. I clothed you in embroidered garments and shod you with blue leather and girded you with fine linen," and so on.

This too can be learned exactly from the writings of the most divine Moses. He prepared the priestly vestments and the holy anointing oil after the God of all had taught him how to make them. In this way let us understand the bracelets on the arms, the necklace on the neck, the ring in the nose, the earrings in the ears, and the crown of boasting set on the head. By the bracelets on the arms he means virtue in action. By the earrings in the ears he means listening to the divine oracles, to which we must cling as the ear holds its earring. By the necklace on the neck he means the ornament of understanding that shines in the governing part of the soul and rests on the heart, hanging from the neck. By the ring in the nose he means the bridle of the divine laws. This is a metaphor taken from bulls, which oxherds lead in this way. For through the prophet Hosea God again says something similar: "Ephraim has run wild like a frenzied heifer." And again: "I heard Ephraim lamenting: You disciplined me, Lord, and I was not disciplined; like a calf I was not trained." So she needed such a bridle, to check her unruly charging.

In the same way let us understand the brothel too. By it he meant the houses of idols. He called each of them a brothel because, although she was joined to God, as it were, and called him her husband, she took pleasure in the wicked demons. She built temples for them and offered them the gifts God had supplied to her. That is why he added: "At the head of every road you built your brothels; you defiled your beauty and spread your legs for every passer-by." By this he points to the excess of her licentiousness. "For you gave yourself not only to those you knew; you drew in all who passed by

[?] “…you mingled licentiously.” Here again he figuratively calls the worship of idols “mingling.” We should note what kind of terms the God of all used when he wished to signify the excess of idolatry: “For you spread your legs to every passer-by and multiplied your harlotry. And you played the harlot with the sons of Egypt, your neighbors, the great of flesh.” Here again he indicated the magnitude of idolatry and the excess of impiety by such terms. “And you were not like a harlot who gathers wages. The adulterous woman is like you, who takes wages from her husband; to all who played the harlot with her she gave wages besides. And you have given wages to all your lovers, and loaded them with gifts, so that they would come to you from all around in your harlotry. And in your harlotry there was perversity in you beyond other women.” By these words, too, he signified that they received from God grain and wine and oil, sheep and oxen and calves, and offered them as sacrifices to idols. They dishonored God, whose gifts these were, and offered them to beings that had never provided anything and brought only destruction; they held out pay to their adulterous lovers but received no pay from them. Similar to these are the words in the prophet Jeremiah: “For now,” he says, “you have committed adultery with wood and with stone. Lift up your eyes and look straight ahead, and see where you have not been defiled. You sat by the roads waiting for them like a lone crow in the desert, and you defiled the land with your harlotries.” And blessed Isaiah says: “How has the faithful city Zion become a harlot, she who was full of justice! Righteousness lodged in her, but now murderers.” And again: “What is this bill of divorce of your mother? Or to which creditor have I sold you? For your iniquities I sent your mother away.” But why should we cite everything the God of all said through the prophets? What has been said is enough to teach us how the divine Scriptures must be understood: we are not to attend to the letter alone, but to unfold its meaning. Having been led, then, from the old bride to the new, let us understand the book of the Song of Songs in this way. Let us abandon those false and harmful opinions and follow the holy Fathers; let us understand one bride conversing with one bridegroom, and learn from the holy apostles who the bridegroom is and who the bride. For the most divine Paul teaches us, writing thus: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.” And he says that the bride is made up of many, for he says, “I betrothed you” in the plural, not “you” in the singular, meaning of course the souls that are pious and perfect in virtue. For the divine word knows the Church as bride, and names Christ the bridegroom. And the great John, who showed

[?] PREFACE [?] the end of the law and the beginning of grace, who stood between the tutor and the wise teacher, in whose time the shadow received the body, says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice.” And the Lord himself calls himself the bridegroom. When the Pharisees found fault with the holy apostles for not fasting, he replied: “The sons of the bridechamber cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them. But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast.” So let us understand the Church as the bride and Christ as the bridegroom. The maidens who follow the bride are souls that are pious and youthful, but have not yet imitated the virtue of the bride or been found worthy of perfection. That is why they follow the bride but are not called brides. The work also contains certain others who are with the bridegroom. Whether one calls them angels, who serve the Master’s command and adorn the bride, or prophets, who proclaimed these things from afar, or apostles, who also serve the Master’s will like angels, one will not miss the mark of the truth. To me, however, they seem rather to be angels. The divine oracles have taught us to understand the bride herself as the souls perfected in virtue, and nothing is more perfect than apostles and prophets except angels; so it seems to me rather that those who serve the bridegroom and are eager to attend the bride are angels. For we find that as soon as the bridegroom was born, an angelic choir rejoiced, was glad, sang hymns and cried out: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will among men.” Gabriel the archangel ministered at the conception itself; it was evidently an angel who commanded Joseph both the flight into Egypt and the return from there; and after the contests against the devil, angels came and ministered to him who had fought on behalf of our weakness and overthrown the adversary, praising him, singing hymns to him, and attending him. At the time of the passion, too, angels were present, strengthening his humanity. Angels keeping watch at the tomb proclaimed his resurrection; and when he was taken up into heaven, angels said to the apostles: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come again in the same way.” That is why it seems to me that the ranks attending the bridegroom are those of angels, who serve the bridegroom’s will and consider the bride worthy of every care. It is also necessary to say this at the outset: we have been taught that there are three works of Solomon, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and

the Song of Songs. Proverbs offers moral benefit to those who desire it. Ecclesiastes explains the nature of visible things and teaches the vanity of the present life, so that, learning how perishable these things are, we may despise them as passing and desire the things to come as abiding. The Song of Songs teaches the mystical union of the bride and the bridegroom. Thus the whole of Solomon’s work is a kind of ladder with three rungs: the moral, the natural and the mystical. For whoever first approaches piety must first have his mind purified by good conduct; next he must perceive the vanity of passing things and the perishability of things that seem pleasant; and from there at last he must take flight and long for the bridegroom, who has promised the eternal goods. That is why this book is placed third, so that one may advance along a path to perfection. I think that the wise Solomon wrote these things having been taught by his father, who was a prophet, and a great prophet. For he certainly heard him singing: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a robe of gold, adorned in many colors.” And again: “Listen, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty, for he is your Lord.” Indeed, they do not allow young men, or those still immature in age, to read it; they bid only those reaching manhood, who are able to understand hidden things and interpret what is written spiritually, to read it. So let us stop quarrelling over whether the book was written prophetically, or whether Solomon, having learned from his father, teaches what he was taught, and let us take up the interpretation. We ask only this of those who will read it: not to accuse us of theft if they find in our interpretations something said by the Fathers. For we confess that we too found in them the starting points for making things clear; and such a thing is not theft but an inheritance from our fathers. Some things we have received from them and set down; others we have discovered ourselves and add. Some things, which certain writers have said at great length, we abridge; others, which need elaboration, we expand. In short, we have undertaken a labor which, I think, will not be useless to those who read it. Therefore we ask those who reap the fruit of our labors without labor to give us their prayers in return for our labors. And if the interpretation should appear inexact, accept at least the labor, and teach what is lacking.

[?] OF THE BLESSED THEODORET, BISHOP OF CYRRHUS, [INTERPRETATION?] OF THE SONG OF SONGS. Since, emboldened by divine grace, we have ventured on the interpretation of this book, let us first of all examine the very title of the book and make it clear: “The Song of Songs, which was sung by Solomon.” Let us consider why the wise Solomon called it not “Song” but “Song of Songs.” For it is clear to all who use sober and pious reasoning that nothing spoken under the working of the divine Spirit is said idly or in vain. This being so, we must consider why this work is called “Song of Songs” and not simply “Song.” Now we find many songs, psalms, hymns and odes spoken and written by blessed David and by the prophets before and after him. The great Moses [?] sang first the ode of victory, when the sea was divided and became a road for the Israelites and a tomb for the Egyptians; second, he sang an ode of thanksgiving, the one at the well; and third, the one in which he recounted the divine gifts and accused the people of their ungrateful disposition. Blessed David, too, sang some hymns of victory and others for the winepresses, some for the morning and others for the evening. But the wise Solomon composes neither a song of victory nor a morning song, but a wedding song. Songs of victory signify the overthrow of enemies and the release of captives, as in: “He makes wars cease to the ends of the earth; he will break the bow and shatter the weapon and burn the shields with fire. Be still, and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth.” This signifies that he shattered the enemies’ armor, freed the captives who had long been subject to them,

made them his own subjects, and was crowned with the kingship of all who willingly accepted him. That is why he says: “I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth.” Of the same kind is: “Clap your hands, all you nations; shout to God with a voice of exultation, for the Lord Most High is awesome, a great king over all the earth.” And again: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one; in your comeliness and your beauty bend your bow, and prosper, and reign.” And again: “Lift up your gates, O rulers, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall come in, the Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.” In these songs, then, the prophets recount the victory of the king and praise him for setting the captives free. But the Song of Songs describes his wedding and depicts his love for the bride. It calls “bride” those who in those songs were released from captivity and obtained freedom, who became intimate with the king, kept an unfading memory of his benefits, showed great goodwill and affection toward him and follow him continually; who then, when the powers above ask, “Who is the King of glory?”, long to be with him and cannot bear to be separated from the one who saved them even for a small part of a day. This is why this book is called the Song of Songs: the phrase signifies that those songs came into being for the sake of this song, and that they lead to it. For this is the sum of all good things and the crowning summit of God’s love for humankind, the ineffable goodness, the measureless mercy, the immeasurable compassion, the inexpressible love: that the Maker and Fashioner and Creator, the Lord and God and Master, who is ever the same, should consent not only to deliver this creature of clay, subject to suffering, corruptible, ungrateful and useless, from death and the tyranny of the devil, but also to grant it freedom; not only to make them free, but also to appoint them sons; not only to bestow the gift of adoption, but also to call her and make her a bride, to be joined to her as a bridegroom, to offer countless wedding gifts, to prepare a bridal chamber and room beforehand, to clothe her who was naked, and to become for her a garment, and food, and drink, and way, and shield, and life, and light, and resurrection. But I am trying to count the sand or the drops of rain, or to measure the sea with a cup, when I dare to grasp God’s love for humankind in words. For this reason, then, the book is called the Song of Songs, because it teaches us the greater forms of God’s goodness
and reveals to us the innermost and inaccessible mysteries, the holy of holies, of God’s love for humankind.

CHAPTER I. 1. [Let him kiss] me with the kisses of his mouth. The bride says this in prayer to the Father of the bridegroom. For she had heard the promises given to Abraham the patriarch and the predictions in Jacob’s blessings. She had heard the great Moses prophesying about him; she had heard the Psalms describing his beauty and power: “You are lovely in beauty beyond the sons of men. Grace is poured out on your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever. Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one. In your comeliness and your beauty bend your bow, and prosper, and reign, for the sake of truth and meekness and righteousness.” She had been taught that this same one, lovely and comely, is both God and the Son who exists before the ages: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; a scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom.” And Isaiah cries out: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with crimson garments from Bozrah? This one, lovely in his robe, with strength.” Having been taught, then, of the bridegroom’s beauty, his strength, his wealth, his kingship, the power he holds over all things, his eternity, his indestructibility, his endlessness, she longs to see him and embrace him, and to give him spiritual kisses. But let none of those who are earthbound and attached to worldly things be scandalized by the word “kisses.” Let him consider that at the time of the mysteries, too, when we receive the members of the bridegroom, we kiss and embrace them and place them on our eyes and our heart; we imagine a kind of bridal embrace, and think that we are with him, embracing and kissing him, since love casts out fear, according to divine Scripture. So the bride longs to be kissed by the bridegroom himself, as if saying to his Father: Send me your only-begotten Son, O Master and Father—for you would rather be called by this name than by that. Long have I waited for him, long have I yearned for him. I have grown weary of receiving his letters through patriarchs, through lawgivers, through prophets. I can no longer bear the flame of love; it is a fire burning and blazing within me. Through all the prophets he promises to come to me, and not even to this day has he been willing to make good his promises. He promised me through David, through Jeremiah, through Isaiah, through Ezekiel and Zechariah and Daniel and the rest of the prophets that he would come and celebrate the wedding.

I do not know why he delays and disregards me in my longing. He said to me through Hosea: “And I will betroth you to myself in righteousness and in justice and in mercy and in compassion, and I will betroth you to myself in faithfulness, and you shall know the Lord.” He said to me through Isaiah: “Rejoice, barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry out, you who are not in labor, for the children of the desolate are many, more than those of her who has a husband.” And every day I wait, longing to obtain what was promised. This is what she hints at when she says: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.” And so that we may not interpret by mere assertion, come, let us call blessed Paul as a witness to what has been said. Writing to the Hebrews and discoursing on faith, he says this about Abraham: “By faith he sojourned in the land of promise as in a foreign land, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of the same promise; for he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose craftsman and builder is God.” And shortly after: “These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them from afar and greeted them, and having confessed that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. For those who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. If they had been thinking of the land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return. But as it is, they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.” And about the great Moses he says that “he chose rather to suffer hardship with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasure of sin, considering the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking to the reward. By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the anger of the king; for he endured as seeing him who is invisible.” And about all the saints together who were distinguished in the Old Testament he says this: “And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had foreseen something better for us, so that apart from us they should not be made perfect.” And the Lord in the holy Gospels says this to the apostles: “Many prophets and kings and righteous men desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear.” And conversing with the Jews he said: “Your father Abraham longed to see my day; and he saw it and was glad.” And Simeon the elder had been divinely told that he would not see death until he had seen the Christ

of the Lord. So when the child had been born and brought up to the temple, Simeon took him in his arms and said: “Now, Master, you dismiss your servant in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples,” and so on. It is clear, then, that because they believed the divine promises they desired to see their fulfillment; and therefore the Song of Songs introduces the bride saying: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.” By “kiss” we understand not a joining of mouths but the communion of a pious soul with the divine Word. The bride seems to be saying something like this: I have heard your words through [the prophets?]; but I long to hear your very voice. I wish to receive teaching directly from your mouth, and to kiss it with the lips of my mind. “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.” As soon as the bride has said this, the bridegroom appears to her, fulfilling that promise: “While you are still speaking, behold, I am here.” And she, at once beholding the one she longed for, is struck with amazement at him, marvels at his breasts and his fragrance, and cries out: 2. Your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices. I know, she says, the ointments prepared by Moses, the oil of anointing and the compounded incense; but of all those spices your ointment is the most fragrant. Here she calls the spiritual grace “ointment”: he is full of it, and from his fullness he has given to us all. That is why blessed Paul also cries out that “we are the fragrance of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to the one a fragrance of death unto death, to the other a fragrance of life unto life.” For just as, for creatures that feed on carrion, foul-smelling bodies are food while ointment is death, so for the impious and for those who have chosen to dwell in the stench of sin, the stench of licentiousness is most pleasant, while the teaching of Christ is heavy and burdensome; and so it brings upon them a death of their own choosing. “For this is the judgment,” he says, “that the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light.” Fittingly, then, the bride says: “And the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.” She does not say “of your ointment” but “of your ointments,” showing that his gifts are many and countless [?]. For, according to blessed Paul, “to one is given a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another the working of mighty deeds, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues.” That is why she does not say “the fragrance of your ointment” but “the fragrance of your ointments.” Having shown his many and varied gifts, she teaches us that from one

…pours forth from a spring. That is why she adds, "Your name is ointment poured out." For these many and various streams, she says, which have filled the whole world with fragrance, have one vein and source: your ointment. "For in him dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead," and in his humanity he received all the gifts of the Spirit together. That is why Isaiah cries out: "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall spring up from his root; and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and godliness; and the spirit of the fear of God shall fill him." This is why she says, "Your name is ointment poured out." She does not simply say "ointment," but "poured out." Ointment hidden in a vessel keeps its fragrance hidden too, but once it is poured out it fills the very air. In the same way Christ the Master was known to few before his passion. But when he endured the cross and death, and the vessel of his body was opened, so to speak, the blessed apostles were at once filled with that fragrance. Then they set off running, travelled over land and sea, carried the preaching to everyone, and filled the whole world with the fragrance. That is why the bride says, "Your name is ointment poured out." For the mere name of Christ is enough to perfume the souls of the godly, as it were, and fill them with every fragrance. If you want to understand it in a more mystical sense, remind yourself of the sacred mystagogy. There those being baptized, after renouncing the tyrant and confessing the King, receive the anointing with the spiritual ointment as a kind of royal seal. In the ointment, as in a type, they receive the invisible grace of the all-holy Spirit. "Therefore the maidens have loved you." (Verse 3.) "They have drawn you; they run after you toward the scent of your ointment." The youthful and courageous souls, she says (for the text calls these "maidens"), have taken hold of this fragrance of your ointment, that is, of your divine and saving teaching. As a result they have loved you so warmly that they draw you to themselves and follow after you. They even do it at a run, so that they will not be left behind or separated from the one they long for. The blessed Paul also points to this race when he says, "I press on, if I may lay hold of that for which I was also laid hold of." And again: "So run," he says, "that you may obtain." And elsewhere: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith." So, then, the souls that have acquired a youthful [?] [Apparatus: … is obvious [?]. "his" is lacking in [?]. "They drew … running": [?] … "of your ointment, running." The received reading at this place is "we will run."]

spirit run. They have fled the soft, languid and slack life and chosen toil over luxury. The fragrance of the ointment charms them and calls them after the bridegroom, and holds them fast, as it were, with an unspeakable bond. The bride says these things, then, while she has not yet been granted the bridal chamber, both to the bridegroom's Father and to the bridegroom himself, who has come to her. But she is also granted the bridal bed and the bridegroom's chambers and storerooms, and in her exultation she says to her own company: "The king has brought me into his chamber." That is, he has revealed his hidden counsels to me. He has made known to me the mystery hidden from the ages and from the generations. He has opened to me the dark, hidden and invisible treasures, as Isaiah prophesied. One can learn this more precisely from the holy Gospels. There Christ the Master spoke to the Jews in parables, but revealed the meaning of the parables to his holy disciples, saying, "To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom, but to them it has not been given." The Lord also calls the mind a "chamber" when he says, "But you, when you pray, go into your chamber and pray to your Father who is in secret." "The king has brought me into his chamber": she is all but saying with the blessed Paul, "What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him, God has revealed to us through his Spirit. For we have the mind of Christ," in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. "The king has brought me into his chamber." We have to ask why the bride alone is brought in, while the maidens are not. They stand outside and wait for the bride who has gone in. When she comes out and tells how the king brought her into his chamber, they add: "Let us rejoice and be glad in you. We will love your breasts more than wine. Uprightness has loved you." Not all who have believed are of equal worth. "For there are many dwelling places with my Father," says Christ, that is, different ranks. The patriarchs form one order and the prophets another. The apostles form one, the martyrs another. Those who have shone in virginity form one, and those who have lawfully taken on the yoke of marriage another. Those who have served God in wealth and proved faithful stewards form one, and those who have bravely endured the many sufferings of poverty another. Those who pursue civic virtue form one, and those who live in the mountains and choose to devote themselves to divine contemplation alone another.

Within these very orders, too, one can find many differences. Some pursue what they pursue more fervently, others more slackly; some more earnestly, others more carelessly. This can also be seen in the Lord's parable. He brings in ten virgins and calls five of them wise and five foolish. The first he admits to the bridal chamber; on the others he shuts the doors. He gives them an answer, out of respect for their virginity, but he does not let them enter, because they neglected the other virtues. Now that we have drawn these distinctions, let us understand the bride as the souls perfected in all the virtues. The maidens who follow her are those who love the bridegroom and strive to follow him, but have not yet imitated the bride's perfection. The Holy Spirit testifies that this is so in Psalm 44, where it says much the same thing. It describes the bridegroom's beauty, the grace on his lips, his eternal blessing, his fearsome armour, the destruction of his enemies, and the submission and worship of the peoples once taken captive. It describes his royal and eternal throne and the scepter of his kingdom, adorned with righteousness. Besides these it describes the human virtue he pursued "when, being in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant." It also describes the anointing he received in his humanity and the gifts the Magi offered. Then it introduces the queen: "The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a robe of gold, adorned in many colours." It calls the souls perfected in virtue "queen," since Paul too says, "If we endure, we shall also reign with him." By the robe of gold and many colours it means the many gifts of the Spirit. Then it also gives her counsel: "Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father's house, and the king will desire your beauty." He shows that he is not only her kinsman in his humanity, but also her Lord and Master in his hidden Godhead. And to remind her of his unspeakable love for mankind, he says, "For he is your Lord and God, and you shall worship him." [?] [Reference: 2 Tim. 2:[?].]

[?]. Then it describes her hidden glory: "For all the glory of the king's daughter is within." For according to the blessed Paul, "Our life is hidden with Christ in God," while in the present life all who want to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted. That is why the blessed Paul cries out: "If in this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are of all people most to be pitied." For this reason it says, "All the glory of the king's daughter is within; she is clothed in golden fringes, adorned in many colours." Here again it calls the various gifts golden, many-coloured fringes. Then it adds: "Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be brought to you; they shall be brought with gladness and rejoicing; they shall be led into the king's temple." It is clear from what has been said, then, who are called the bride. They are those who have attained to the perfect man, to the measure of stature, as the blessed Paul puts it, and have acquired the perfection of virtue. Those who have not yet attained perfection, and fall short of these, follow the bride like maidens and show every kindness and affection to her and to the bridegroom. "The king has brought me into his chamber. Let us rejoice and be glad in you." For they are not jealous or envious, though they remain outside and have not yet gained the bridal chamber. Instead they are glad and rejoice and [?] at the bride's honour, and they are content to enjoy her sweetest voice. Then they add: "We will love your breasts more than wine." What she said to the bridegroom, they say to the bride. Through their kindness and affection toward her they win the bridegroom's kindness. For Christ too says to the apostles, "Whoever receives you receives me"; and, "Whoever gives one of these little ones who believe in me a cup of cold water to drink, truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward." By the bride's breasts, again, the maidens mean the streams of teaching, which pour out waters suited to every age. They promise to love the bride's breasts more than [?] wine. For [?] figuratively it is called wine, which gladdens the human heart. One can learn that these things happened in both the Old and the New Testament, and one can see them happening every day. For in the Old Testament God revealed the things to come to the prophets and
taught them. They enjoyed God's chambers and hidden things, and then went out and told people what had been revealed and made known to them. That is why David says to God: "The unknown and hidden

things of your wisdom you have made known to me." Those who enjoyed the divine streams through the prophets looked to the prophets as mediators between God and human beings. The apostles likewise, inspired by God, kept carrying the preaching of godliness to all people. The apostles enjoyed the Master's chambers, and their hearers received the apostolic streams, as if from breasts more precious than all wine and all gladness. In the present time, too, the teachers of the Church offer the divine streams to the people as if from chambers. The one who enjoys them draws spiritual nourishment as if from breasts, and considers it better than every gladness of this life. That is why in the Song the bride says, "The king has brought me into his chamber." And the maidens [?]

add: "Uprightness has loved you." For "the Lord is good and upright," as the blessed David says, and "a scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom," and for this reason he has loved you. If so, it is fitting for us too to cling to you, attend on you constantly, and enjoy your breasts. Then the bride speaks again: (4) "I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon. (5) Do not look at me because I have been blackened, because the sun has looked askance at me." I think the bride is no longer saying this to the maidens. She is saying it to those who pride themselves on the law, preen themselves on the Old Testament and are haughty. They reproach her not only with her foreign birth but also with her former superstition and the black complexion that came from it. So she says to them: I am not only black, but also beautiful. Long blind and dressed in old rags, I have recovered my sight. Now, clothed in a robe of gold and adorned in many colours, I have obtained royal rank and stand beside the king. I have thrust you out, you who raged against the king, handed him over to death, and defiled the bridal chamber with a crowd of adulterers. So do not reproach me with the blackness of my complexion, and do not bring my former wrongs out into the open. I am black, I admit, but I am beautiful and pleasing to the bridegroom. Be afraid of Miriam's example. She too reproached Moses for marrying an Ethiopian woman, and she became leprous, white as snow. As one unclean she was put out of the camp and did not come back in until she repented. So I too am an Ethiopian, but I am the bride of the great Lawgiver. I am the daughter of a priest of Midian, an idolater; but I forgot my people and my father's house, and so the king desired my beauty. So do not look at me because I have been blackened, because the sun has looked askance at me. You will see me, who am now blackened, made white, and you will cry out: "Who is this

who comes up made white?" I will also tell you the cause of this blackening. I was blackened by serving the creature rather than the Creator, and by worshipping this visible sun instead of the Sun of righteousness. But I saw the difference between the one and the other, left the thing made, and worshipped the Maker. "So do not look at me because I have been blackened, because the sun has looked askance at me," or, as Symmachus has it, "because the sun has scorched me." "For I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem": black because of my former ungodliness, beautiful because of my repentance; black because of unbelief, beautiful because of faith. I was as utterly black as the tents of Kedar, a name that means "darkness." And I have become as beautiful as the curtains of Solomon, that is, as Solomon's tents, as Solomon's garments. Of these the Lord says, "Consider the lilies of the field, which neither spin nor weave, yet your heavenly Father clothes them. Truly I tell you, not even Solomon in all his glory was arrayed like one of these." That is why, a little later, the bridegroom calls her a lily. She neither spins nor weaves, but leads a life free of care, and the bridegroom himself clothes and feeds her. So the bride says: Formerly I was likened to the tents of Kedar, which means "darkness." I was enslaved to darkness and served demons. Now I have suddenly been changed, and I resemble the curtains of Solomon. For she has become not only the bride but also the temple of Christ, the peaceable one. "My mother's sons fought in me." This too is connected with what came before. She teaches the daughters of Jerusalem how, though black and ill-favoured, she suddenly became beautiful. "For my mother's sons," she says, "fought in me." By sons she means the holy apostles. Of them the Holy Spirit says in Psalm 44 to the queen herself: "In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will make them rulers over all the earth." By her mother, and theirs, she means the Jerusalem above, of which the blessed Paul says, "But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is the mother of us all." "So my mother's sons," she says, "fought in me." She means the war the apostles waged against idolatry and every other kind of lawlessness. In each of their hearers they took on a kind of battle and war, striving to drive the wicked habits out of souls and to plant the laws of godliness firmly in them. To learn more clearly how the blessed heralds of godliness fought in the souls of their disciples, let us listen to the blessed

Stephen as he fights and says: "You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you." And the blessed Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: "It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, of a kind not even named among the Gentiles." And again: "I fear that when I come to you my God may humble me, and I may mourn over many who sinned before and have not repented." Writing to the Galatians, he says: "O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you so that you do not obey the truth, you before whose eyes Jesus Christ was portrayed among you as crucified?" In this way the first interpreters and heralds of godliness rebuked and exhorted. They smoothed out the wrinkles of sins and scraped away aged habits. So they made the Lord's bride new instead of old, comely instead of ugly and hideous, and whitest of all instead of black. That is why the bride, wishing to show how she became lovely and beautiful, says: "My mother's sons fought in me; they made me keeper in the vineyards." For they handed over to me the divine commandments as vineyards, so to speak. They urged me not only to work and cultivate them but also to guard them, so that no wicked beast would ravage the fruit. To this she adds: "My own vineyard I did not keep." The saying has two meanings, both godly and full of benefit. It may mean: My former vineyard, which I cultivated before I came to faith and which my fathers handed down to me, I have left untended and unguarded, so that those former things are now utterly destroyed and consigned to oblivion. Or it may mean: I neglected my own vineyard, that is, the benefit of my own soul, and preferred the gains of others to my own. This is what the blessed Paul says: "Love does not seek its own." And again: "Let no one seek his own good, but each the good of the other." And of himself he says: "I do not seek my own advantage, but that of the many, that they may be saved." I have set down both interpretations so that readers may know both and take whichever seems truer to them. After this the bride leaves off her words to the maidens and her teaching to the daughters of Jerusalem. She turns to the bridegroom, lays bare the love she has for him, and says: (6) "Tell me, you whom my soul has loved," [Reference: Gal. 3:1.]

…following the image of that occupation, she entreats [?], saying: “Since my soul has loved you, tell me where you pasture at the time of noon, or where you make the sheep lie down; so that I do not wander here and there in ignorance, and, straying and roaming, fall in with flocks that have not been granted your care but have other herdsmen and cattle-keepers.” For where the text has “veiled,” Symmachus put “wandering.” And it is fitting that the bride asks at the time of noon where the bridegroom stays, since [?] the light of knowledge [?]. For this reason she is anxious and longs to learn the place of the bridegroom where he makes the sheep lie down at noon, so that she may not fall in with the flocks of those who are called his companions. We should know that, just as there were prophets and, opposed to them, false prophets, and again apostles and, holding the opposite views, false apostles, so too divine Scripture speaks of false christs. That is why the Lord says, “Many false prophets will arise and will lead many astray.” And blessed Paul knows how to speak not only of false brothers but also of false apostles. That is why he says, “For such men are false apostles.” The bride begs not to fall in with these, since they put on the outward form of shepherds and are seen to have flocks and folds as well. Such are those who hold the views of Arius, Eunomius, Marcion, Valentinus, Mani and Montanus: they wear the outward form and name of Christians, they build churches, they read the divine Scriptures to sheep they have led astray, they pasture badly those who follow them, and they are thought to be the bridegroom's companions, yet they are treacherous and deadly, holding out poisons to the sheep instead of nourishing grass. That is why the bride begs the bridegroom to show her where he makes the sheep lie down at noon, so that she may not become “veiled” — or “wandering,” as Symmachus has it — beside the flocks of those who are called his companions but are in fact his enemies. So the bridegroom answers the bride and says: 7. “If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out in the footsteps of the flocks, and pasture your kids by the tents of the shepherds.” What he means is this: Look to yourself and examine what concerns you — for you have become beautiful, the comeliest of all women — and recognize those who are like you. But if you have not known yourself, search out the tracks of the flocks, and follow them, and pasture not only the sheep but also your kids by the tents of the shepherds. For the Master who loves humankind wants not only the righteous but also sinners to be counted worthy of every

care. That is why he says, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick,” and, “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” And through Ezekiel the prophet he says, “I do not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he should turn and live.” And the blessed apostle Paul says of him, “Who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” For this reason he wants her to feed the kids as well. Divine Scripture takes kids as a figure of sinners: the Lord said that these would stand on the left, separated from the lambs who have been allotted the place on the right. And in the law, too, it was not a sheep but a he-goat from the goats that was offered for sin. That is why the bridegroom says to the bride: Follow the tracks of the flocks and search out the life of the saints who went before; and by the tents of those shepherds — that is, in the apostolic churches — feed your kids, since you have heard in the holy Gospels: “See that you do not despise one of the least of these little ones who believe in me; for truly I tell you, their angels see the face of your Father in heaven every day.” 8. “To my mare among Pharaoh's chariots I have likened you, my close one.” Here he figuratively calls “Pharaoh” the destroyer of our nature, the accursed one and our common enemy, whom he has sunk, like Pharaoh, beneath the holy waters of baptism. So: I judge you, who have come close to me and acquired love for me, to be like my mare, which I used when I drowned Pharaoh's chariots. He used the form of a servant as a kind of vehicle — the form he took when he emptied himself — so that he might work salvation for the whole race. It is to this mare, then, that he likens the bride. And the Apostle bears witness to this meaning when he speaks thus of Christ the Savior: “Who will transform the body of our humiliation so that it may be conformed to the body of his glory.” And again: “And we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Lord, the Spirit.” From the apostolic words, then, let us understand the mystical sayings of the Song, and let us hear the bridegroom saying: You, who have come close to me and are therefore called “close,” and who reap that name from the fact itself, I say are like my mare, which I used to drown the spiritual Pharaoh with his chariots, and I gave you freedom. To this he adds:

“[?] your [neck] like necklaces!” But again, let us not understand the cheeks and the neck in a fleshly way. Let us bear in mind that divine Scripture often uses bodily names also of the soul. At one point the prophet Jeremiah says, “My belly, my belly, I am in pain,” and to show that he is not speaking of this belly he adds, “and the senses of my heart.” And when blessed Paul says, “Lift up the drooping hands and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed,” blessed Paul was not exhorting them about hands, or knees, or visible lameness; by these names he was speaking of the practical activities of the soul. [?] So let us understand [?]: “Your cheeks are lovely as a turtledove's, your neck like necklaces.” For the Church, being made up of many men and women, has some who are called cheeks, some eyes, some ears, some mouth, others hands, and others feet. So the bridegroom praises those who pursue modesty and possess the blush of shame, and he says, “Your cheeks are lovely as a turtledove's.” Those who have written about the natures of animals say that the turtledove not only loves solitude but is also chaste: the male joins himself to one female, and the female keeps company with one male, and even after the death of its mate it will not endure to be joined to another. Fittingly, then, he says that the Church is like this bird: she has been joined to Christ, has fled union with others, and would not endure to forsake him even after his death, but awaited his resurrection and awaits his second coming. And he says that her neck is like necklaces. This is a collar, a kind of ornament that beautifies the neck. He praises her for drawing well the yoke of godliness, of which the bridegroom says in the Gospels: “Take my yoke upon you, for my yoke is easy and my burden light.” That is why in the Song he admires the neck that bears this yoke, as one that [does not need?] outward adornment and added beauty but has its comeliness from within, so that even bare it is like the necklaces with which others adorn their necks [?]. When the bridegroom had said these things, the bridegroom's attendants and servants also answer and say to the bride: 10, 11. “We will make you likenesses of gold with studs of silver, until the king is at his reclining.” They seem to me to indicate here the [?] before the coming of Christ the Master

time, and they console the bride: Throughout the whole time before the king rises, we will be with you and adorn you with what adornment we can; and we will not leave you until he rises, but will bring you likenesses of gold and studs of silver. It was consistent for them to say “likenesses of gold” and not gold itself, since the bridegroom's gifts are greater, while those of his ministers do not have equal glory. That is why we pay greater honor to the divine Gospels, though we also honor the law and the prophets and the writings of the holy apostles. Fittingly, then, the bridegroom's ministers said, “We will make you likenesses of gold with studs of silver, until the king is at his reclining.” By studs of silver and likenesses of gold let us understand the variety of the gifts of grace and of the providence that God exercises over us. For we also enjoy help from angels: “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and will deliver them.” And: “He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways.” And the law itself was given through the ministry of angels. That is why the Apostle says, “For if the word spoken through angels proved firm.” So as long as the king reclines and until he rises, we, they say, will bring what we can. By his “reclining” they mean his death. That is why Balaam too, prophesying, says, “A man will come forth from his seed and will rule over many nations,” and a little later: “He lay down and rested like a lion, and like a lion's cub; who will rouse him? Those who bless you are blessed, and those who curse you are cursed.” These words can also be found in the prophecy that the patriarch Jacob spoke to Judah. After the bridegroom's ministers had spoken thus, the bride says again: “My nard gave forth its fragrance. 12. My kinsman is to me a bundle of myrrh.” We must first ask why she calls him her kinsman. We have been taught that the bride is the Church from the nations; but the bridegroom's earlier wife was the multitude of the Jews, who received a certificate of divorce into her hands because of her own licentiousness. They are sisters, since both boast of Adam as their father; but the bridegroom sprang from the former according to his humanity. For blessed Paul says, “It is evident that our Lord has sprung from Judah.” And again: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. It does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as of many, but as of one: ‘And to your seed,’ who is Christ.” And concerning David blessed Peter says that “being a

prophet, and knowing that God had sworn an oath to him that from the fruit of his loins he would raise up the Christ according to the flesh, he foresaw and spoke of his death, that ‘his soul was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption.’” Since, then, the multitude of the Jews and the Church from the nations are sisters, and Christ is the son of the former according to the flesh, the bride fittingly calls him her kinsman, as one who became her sister's son according to his humanity. This kinsman of mine, then, is to me both nard and a bundle of myrrh. I call him by many names, enchanted by the fragrance of his ointment, and I cannot make do with one name. Indeed, the power of his fragrance surpasses all names together; but, overcome by love for him, I name him nard and call him a bundle of myrrh. Nard, because he was anointed with the costly pure nard whose fragrance filled the whole house — a figure of the inhabited world; for the service offered to the Lord by the godly has filled the world with the sweet fragrance of faith. And I call him a bundle of myrrh-drops, since he himself “came down like rain upon a fleece, and like drops falling upon the earth.” The prophets also called him a drop: “For,” it says, “from the drop of this people Jacob will surely be gathered.” We should know that Symmachus and Aquila called the myrrh-drops “myrrh.” Myrrh signifies the bridegroom's death and the fragrance that came from it to the bride. And she added: “He will lodge between my breasts” — that is, in the ruling part of my soul, which rests in the heart lying between the breasts. The fulfilment of the prophecy spoken by God shows this: “I will dwell among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people, says the Lord Almighty.” And the bridegroom himself promises, saying, “I and the Father will come and make our dwelling with him.” That is why Paul too cries out, “Or do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” For this reason the bride says, “He will lodge between my breasts.” 13. “My kinsman is to me a cluster of cypros in the vineyards of Engedi.” At a loss as to what name to give the bridegroom, the bride ranges here and there, gathering titles from every quarter and bestowing them on him: love urges her to name him, yet she cannot find a worthy title. That is why she now calls him a cluster of cypros, that is, “in bloom,” meaning just beginning to flower; for the vine is fragrant at that season. And she adds

“in the vineyards of Engedi” — this is how fragrant it is. If the name means the place in Judea, famous for its marvelous vineyards, it should be understood figuratively thus: Your cluster is more fragrant than those vines. But if she used the name “Engedi” for its meaning — it is interpreted “eye of trial” — it should be understood thus: Even while I am amid trials and attacked by many, I take hold of your fragrance; and above the vineyards that flourish at the present time — understood figuratively, and lying in the midst of trial, for “the life of man on earth is a trial” — I prefer the fragrance of the blossoming cluster. And if the cluster just in bloom is like this, consider what it is like when it is ripening; and if the ripening one is better than this, reflect on what the fully ripe one is like, ready for the winepress. For I think that the same one, in proportion to the stages of spiritual growth, is in blossom for some, unripe for others, ripening for others, fully ripe for others, and is drunk by the perfect: “For your cup that inebriates is like the very best.” When the bride had said these things, the bridegroom again converses with her and says: 14. “Behold, you are beautiful, my close one; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves.” Again he praises her beauty and admires her loveliness, and by the repetition he expresses his amazement at her comeliness. Above all he extols her eyes, saying, “Your eyes are doves,” that is, spiritual; for the Holy Spirit came down in the form of a dove and rested on the bridegroom. That is why he does not say “like a dove's,” but “doves” — that is, spiritual, filled with divine grace, free from mist, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face as in a mirror, being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Lord, the Spirit, and able to say, “But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit.” The bride answers again and says: 15, 16. “Behold, you are beautiful, my kinsman, and comely, by our shaded bed. The beams of our houses are cedars, our rafters cypresses.” Up to now she had continued to admire his fragrance; but now she is amazed at his beauty as well, her eyes having been enlightened, and [?]

[?] seeds; and she who receives them conceives, carries in the womb, suffers labor pains, and cries out with the prophet: “Because of the fear of you, Lord, we conceived in the womb, and were in labor, and brought forth the spirit of your salvation, which we have conceived upon the earth.” She calls the bed “shaded” because it is helped by the grace of the Spirit and set free from the scorching heat of sin. For what the cloud was to Israel, the help of the Spirit is to us. That is why she says, “By our shaded bed. The beams of our houses are cedars, our rafters cypresses.” She chose these kinds of wood because the cedar does not rot, and the cypress is fragrant. Both qualities are to be found in divine Scripture, which is for us not only a bed but also a house, a table and food; and it not only offers fragrance but also promises incorruption, freedom from suffering and immortality. And if anyone wishes to call the churches throughout every land and sea the houses of the bride, he will not miss the truth, the cedars and cypresses being understood figuratively: the more honorable as the beams — for the beams bear the roof — and the lesser as what are called rafters. Praised in this way by the bride, the bridegroom teaches her that she has not yet beheld his true beauty, but has so far delighted only in the shadow of that beauty.

1. “For I,” he says, “am a flower of the plain, a lily of the hollows.” You have seen my human comeliness, he says, since no one has ever seen God. For I became a flower of the plain — that is, I took up an earthly body and sprang up on the earth, though I exist before the ages and am exalted, or rather immeasurable. I became a lily not of mountains, nor of hills, nor simply of plains, but of hollows. For he proclaimed the good news not only of salvation to the living but also of resurrection to the dead, descending into the lower parts of the earth so that he might fill all things. That is why he calls himself a flower of the plain, but a lily of the hollows, that is, of the dead; for to them too he both promised and accomplished the return to life. Then, having called himself by such names, he says to the bride: 2. “As a lily among thorns, so is my close one among the daughters.” For as great as the difference is between the lily and the thorns, so far does your beauty surpass that of the daughters, who are called by this name because they were counted worthy of the calling, but had deprived themselves of being chosen. “For many,” he says, “are called, but few are chosen.”

The prophet Isaiah also calls the bride by this name, saying: “Rejoice, thirsty wilderness; let the wilderness rejoice and blossom like a lily.” For she who is called the bride was formerly a wilderness, fruitless and waterless, and had no shaded bed; but she [longed for?] the bridegroom, which is why she cries out, “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.” And the prophet, knowing this — for he was a spiritual man — said, “Rejoice, thirsty wilderness; let the wilderness rejoice and blossom like a lily.” That is why the bridegroom too says to her, “As a lily among thorns, so is my close one among the daughters.” Here he seems to call the churches of the heretics daughters because of his calling of them, not because of their own choice. Those he likens to thorns, but her to a fragrant lily, which has brightness on the outside and its golden bloom set in the middle. Such is the soul that is clothed in the brightness of righteousness and carries within, hidden in its inner chambers, the spiritual gift of wisdom and knowledge. The bride answers the bridegroom and says to him: 3. “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my kinsman among the sons. In his shade I desired, and I sat down, and his fruit was sweet in my throat.” Great is the difference between the apple and the lily: the lily delights only sight and smell, while the apple, besides sight and smell, offers pleasure to the taste as well for those who want it. For it is edible, and is eaten. That is why the bride is called a lily and the bridegroom an apple: he is eaten and becomes food for the bride, while she is not eaten but has only fragrance. That is why she says, “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my kinsman among the sons.” By “sons,” as by “daughters” earlier, she means those who were counted worthy of the calling but made themselves unworthy of being chosen; these, the bride says, are like trees of the forest and fruitless trees. But she calls the bridegroom an apple, which is smooth to the touch, sweet to the taste, fragrant to the smell, most delightful and charming to the sight, and most pleasant to the hearing; for as soon as we hear, we bring all our senses to the word. Such is our Master, Savior and bridegroom: he feasts all our senses. The bride says that she desired to sit in his shade and did so; and after this she says that she also partook of his fruit, and that it proved most sweet in her throat. For she wants to escape the rays of wickedness, which know how to scorch, so that she may not become black again. The shadow of the bridegroom is what now appears in a mirror and in a riddle, as blessed Paul says: “For now I see as in a mirror, and as

…in a riddle, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.” That is why she says, “In his shade I longed, and I sat down, and his fruit was sweet in my throat.” For sitting under his shade I gather his fruit and partake of it; and the initiated bear witness to this, as they delight in the bridegroom’s limbs.

2:4–5. “Bring me into the house of wine; set love upon me. Strengthen me with perfumes, heap me round with apples, for I am wounded with love.” By the house of wine I think she means the divine winepresses, about which the prophet says: “How lovely are your dwellings, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord.” For having entitled the psalm “For the winepresses,” he went on to say this, teaching that he calls the churches of God winepresses.
