In them the spiritual wine is pressed out and, as it were, trodden, and it gladdens the souls of the pious, according to the prophecy that says: “They shall be drunk with the richness of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight.” That is why the bride asks to enter his house of wine, and appeals to the bridegroom’s attendants, saying, “Set love upon me”: that is, teach me the way of love, so that I may not love father or mother more than the bridegroom, or field, or vineyards, and so prove unworthy of the bridal chamber. For he himself declared: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves sons or daughters more than me is not worthy of me.” And the ancient law given to Adam said the same: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.” “Set love upon me,” then, so that I may be joined to my bridegroom and prefer him to father and mother and everything else. “Strengthen me with perfumes”: that is, make me firm with the bridegroom’s fragrance and prop me up, so that nothing may shake me, by continually bringing me that sweet scent, lest I forget the bridegroom and wander off after other things. And also, “Heap me round with apples,” meaning, load me with the bridegroom’s fruits, so that, sitting under his shade, breathing his perfumes and laden with his fruit, I may keep the memory of him unforgotten. “For I am wounded by love of him.” For he is a chosen arrow, and he wounds the souls he strikes.

2:6. “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” But let us not fall back into bodily notions when we hear of left and right. For about wisdom too, which is a state and not a substance, Solomon says

that “Length of life and years of living are in her right hand, and in her left are wealth and glory.” And about embracing, again, one can find it said in Proverbs: “Love her, and she will guard you; put a fence around her, and she will exalt you; honour her, so that she may embrace you.” Taking our starting point from here, then, let us understand these words too in a more spiritual way, believing that what is called the embrace is the communion of the divine Word with the pious soul; and left and right must be understood as terms borrowed from our own condition. But so as not to leave the matter unexamined, let us understand it like this. God knows how both to do good and to punish, assigning each to those who deserve it. So, taking the right hand to mean his beneficent grace and the left his power to punish, let us hear the bride saying, “His left hand is over my head”: that is, I am above punishments and not subject to them, because I have drawn near to the bridegroom and devoted myself to his service. “His right hand will embrace me” means: he will adorn me with his benefits and fill me with them, as though enfolding and embracing me, and fulfilling my desire. Blessed Paul was pointing to this when he said, “And so we shall always be with the Lord.” May it be granted to us too never to experience his power to punish nor to taste the punishments he has threatened, but to enjoy the gifts he has promised, by the grace and love for humankind of the bridegroom, Christ our Lord, to whom be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.

…they urge people to share their love with them. That is why in the Song of Songs too the bride, having described the bridegroom’s embrace (“His left hand is under my head”) and having said, “and his right hand will embrace me,” cannot bear to delight in the bridegroom alone, nor does she think it enough to enjoy those holy arms by herself. Instead she urges the maidens as well; and she does not merely urge them but compels them, and lays on them the constraint of an oath, that they should rouse and awaken love until the bridegroom wills. She calls them daughters of Jerusalem, clearly the heavenly Jerusalem, of which blessed Paul says: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is the mother of us all.” By the field she means the world; for so too the Lord in the holy Gospels, interpreting a parable, says, “The field is the world.” By the powers and strengths of the field she means the angelic powers that go about the world at God’s will; or else the holy prophets and apostles, who, filled with the divine Spirit and travelling through the whole inhabited world, drove out the demons who oppose God and hate him, and planted godliness in human souls. So the bride, having come to enjoy the bridegroom and having learned that unspeakable delight by experience, cries out: “I have charged you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field, that you rouse and awaken love until it pleases.” That is: do not let your love for God fall asleep within you, but rouse it and kindle it, and pour on it the memory of his benefits as though it were oil, so that it may not be said of us too, “They slept their sleep and found nothing.” For if you do not proclaim his salvation day after day, and do not remember the wonders he has done, but forget his benefits, love will be quenched and, as it were, die. You must constantly kindle it, rouse it, and raise its flame on high. And the measure of love is to be the bridegroom’s will. So do not stop rousing it and kindling its fire until the bridegroom says it has reached its measure. Like this is what blessed Paul wrote to the Corinthians, and through the Corinthians to all of us: “Keep watch, stand firm in the faith, be courageous, be strong; let everything you do be done in love.” And at the end of the letter he says: “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be accursed.” Those who love the Saviour fervently love him so much that they loathe those unwilling to love him as they would stinking, rotting corpses. This is what blessed David means

when he says: “Did I not hate those who hate you, Lord, and waste away over your enemies? I hated them with a perfect hatred; they became my enemies.” And of those who love him he says: “But to me your friends, O God, are greatly honoured; their rule has been greatly strengthened.” The blessed men were taught by the God of all to love in this way those who love the one they love. For he himself first said to Abraham: “I will bless those who bless you, and those who curse you I will curse.” And he says to Israel: “I will be an enemy to your enemies, and I will oppose those who oppose you.” From this David was taught to say those words, and blessed Paul to declare accursed those who do not love the Lord. That is why the bride too charges the daughters of Jerusalem to rouse and awaken love for the bridegroom until he himself wills. Speaking these words to the maidens, and [urging] them to a love like her own

2:8. “The voice of my beloved.” Having grown familiar with his holy words, she recognizes his voice, as the Lord too says in the holy Gospels: “My sheep hear my voice,” but they will not follow a stranger, because they do not know the voice of strangers. So the bride knows the bridegroom’s voice; she knows the difference between an adulterer and a bridegroom. She loathes the voices of adulterers, wolves and hirelings, but she longs for the words of the bridegroom and shepherd. That is why, as soon as she senses his presence, she cries out, “The voice of my beloved,” and cannot bear to stay seated, but rises, watches eagerly, looks all around, and on seeing him cries: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.”

2:9. “My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of Bethel.” It is worth asking why she likens him to a gazelle and a young stag, what the mountains of Bethel are, what the leaps and the bounds are, and what the hills and mountains are on which these take place. They say that the gazelle (dorkas) is named for its keen sight (oxydorkia), and received this name because it sees sharply. They also say that deer destroy creeping creatures, and eat snakes, vipers and all other such things as though they were grass, and suffer no harm from it. Since, then, Christ the Master, in his humanity, is the rod that came forth from the root of Jesse, and the Spirit of God rested upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and godliness, and

the spirit of the fear of God shall fill him, the bride likens him to a gazelle because of his keen and penetrating sight and his foreknowledge of things to come. And again she says he is like a young stag, since he crushed the heads of the dragons upon the water, and shattered the heads of the dragon, and likewise slew with the sword the crooked serpent and the dragon that is in the sea. He gave his disciples authority to tread upon snakes and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy; and although he committed no sin, he took away the sins of the world and consumed them as though they were snakes. She likens him to a young stag because he is called not only man but also Son of Man, and not only lion but also lion’s whelp: “For having lain down,” it says, “he slept like a lion and like a lion’s whelp.” It is likely, too, that she is hinting that while he was still small in bodily age he consumed the power of the devil as if it were snakes, and as soon as he was born drew the magi, the devil’s spokesmen, to worship him.

Under the law both the gazelle and the deer are clean animals. The gazelle is placed before the deer because its keen sight makes it a figure of faith. For whoever comes to God must first believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him. Divine Scripture also speaks of deer. At one point blessed David says in Psalm 17: “It is God who girds me with power and has made my way blameless, perfecting my feet like a deer’s.” For my way became blameless, he says, since my feet were perfected like a deer’s; for I was able to tread upon snakes and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy. At another point, in Psalm 28, he says: “The voice of the Lord perfects the deer and will lay bare the thickets.” Here he calls the holy apostles deer. Their feet are beautiful, since they bring good news of good things and trample the deadly snakes that plot against human souls. Through them the barren thickets, the deceit of the idols, were laid bare; through them everyone in the temple of God says, “Glory.” The blessed prophet Habakkuk says such things too: “The Lord my God is my strength; he will set my feet like a deer’s and set me upon the heights, so that I may conquer in his song.”

But it is time to return to the matter in hand. “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills. My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of Bethel.” Here the bride teaches that the overthrow of the idols was brought about by the bridegroom. For by mountains and

hills she means the groves and sacred precincts of the demons that once stood on the mountains. Leaping and bounding against them by the wisdom of his words and the power of his miracles, he overcame them and made them vanish completely. Indeed Symmachus too, rendering this more clearly, says: “Behold, he comes, striding over the mountains, leaping across the hills.” To this the bride adds again: “Behold, he stands behind our wall, peering through the windows, looking in through the lattices.” She teaches that, having brought low every mountain and hill according to Isaiah’s prophecy, he comes to her, who was long lowly and likened to a ravine, and fills her, and makes the crooked straight and the rough places into smooth roads. And he puts a wall around her: as around a city, so that she may not be besieged by enemies; and as around a vineyard, a garden and a paradise, so that not everyone who passes along the road may pluck her fruit, nor the boar from the forest ravage her, nor the solitary wild beast feed on her, as happened to that earlier vine transplanted from Egypt. She signifies, then, that having destroyed the precincts of the demons and the groves and temples of the so-called gods, he has come to her. (This is what she hinted at with “upon the mountains of Bethel”; for Bethel means “house of God,” and the impious called those who are not gods by the same name as the God who is over all.) He has not yet entered her chamber, but stands outside the wall and peers through the windows; and by windows she means the senses. For through the senses, as through windows, both good things and their opposites flow into the soul, and flow out from it again. That is why the prophet Jeremiah says, “Death has come up through the windows.” For “whoever looks at a woman so as to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart,” and death enters through the windows. And whoever accepts an idle report accepts death through the windows. But the bride now enjoys the bridegroom’s beauty through the windows. We must ask, then, how the bridegroom peers through the windows, that is, through our senses. When we meditate on the law of the Lord day and night and delight in the divine words, and attend to what is written with compunction and understanding, we open our

…and surrounded by nets, but he rescues her “from the snare of the hunters and from a troubling word.” And in the very midst of temptations he peeps out through the nets, cheers her when she is besieged, and lifts up her spirit. One can find this done by the God of all in both the Old and the New Scripture, and find the pious receiving every consolation from the God of all. He allowed Sarah to be carried off by Pharaoh, but he peered through the nets and cheered the patriarch Abraham, and, tearing the nets apart, returned the prey to him safe and sound. She was caught again, by Abimelech, and again he peers through the nets, and he not only saved the prey but also did good to the hunter. He did this for Isaac too, who suffered over Rebekah what his father had suffered over Sarah. He did this for Jacob as well: when his father-in-law was eager to overtake him and bent on killing him, he appears again through the nets, encouraging Jacob and frightening Laban. And again, when Jacob feared his brother’s approach, he appears, drives out his fear and fills him with courage. Joseph too, when he was sold into slavery and became a servant, he stayed with in his master’s house and was present with in prison, and everywhere he kept peering through the nets and cheering him. To pass over the saints in between and avoid a lengthy discourse: so he cheered the most wise Daniel when he was handed over to the lions, and, peering out from the nets, gave him courage. So he went into that fearful furnace with those blessed youths. So he urged the holy apostles, when they had been thrown into prison by the Jews, to take courage and preach the word of godliness boldly. So afterwards, when blessed Paul was held prisoner in Jerusalem and expecting death, he gave him courage, saying: “Take courage, Paul; for as you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify in Rome as well.” Hinting at this too, the bride says:

2:10. “My beloved answers and says to me: Arise, come, my close one, my fair one, my dove.” The bridegroom bears witness to the bride’s beauty. He does not simply call her fair, but “my fair one,” showing that her beauty pleases him greatly. He also calls her a dove, hinting by this name at spiritual grace;

for the Holy Spirit came upon him in the form of a dove. Blessed Paul is accustomed to call the perfect “spiritual.” So, writing to those still imperfect, he says: “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ.” But to the perfect he writes: “You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you.” Fittingly, then, the bridegroom calls the soul that has been perfected in virtue a dove, that is, spiritual and filled with the Holy Spirit. For the prophet Isaiah too, foreseeing this from afar, saw the holy apostles flying about the whole world as if they had wings, and their disciples and hearers following them like nestlings, and he cries out: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves with their young?” So here too the bridegroom cheers and consoles his Church as she struggles in temptations, peering through the windows and peeping out from the nets, and he bids her rise and fly up to him. For he has given her the wings of that dove of which blessed David says: “If you lie down among the lots, there are the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her back with the sheen of gold.” By lots he means the two Testaments; by the dove, the grace of the Spirit; by her silvered wings, the brilliance of the word; and by the back with the sheen of gold, the splendour of the hidden mysteries. For if, he says, you rest between the two Testaments and draw benefit from both, you will find there the manifold gifts of the Spirit. So the bride, having received the spiritual exhortation and lain down among the lots, found the silvered wings by which she is bidden to fly up to the bridegroom.

2:11–13. “For behold,” he says, “the winter is past, the rain is over, it has gone its way. The flowers have appeared in the land; the time of pruning has come; the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land. The fig tree has put forth its unripe figs; the vines are in blossom, they have given off their fragrance.” Let us set beside these words, if you will, the Gospel [words] of the

[?] has passed." He calls the time before his coming winter, and the time after his coming spring, and the expected age the height of summer. That is why he says, "The winter has passed, and the rain": the threats of the law and the severe punishments for sins. "It has gone away by itself." For the shadow gives way to the body, and the tutor to the wise teacher. "For the flowers have appeared in the land." We must pay attention to the precision of the words. He did not say fruits, but flowers. For the perfection of good things is granted to the worthy in the age to come, but here, as blessed Paul says, "Now I see as in a mirror, in a riddle, but then face to face." Moreover, "the time of cutting has come," or, as Symmachus and Aquila have it, "of pruning." For after the coming of Christ all the nations have received this cleansing. That is why the Lord says, "I am the true vine, you are the branches; my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every one that bears fruit he prunes, so that it may bear more fruit." For this reason he says, "And the time of cutting has come." "The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land." Here again he calls the teaching of the all-holy Spirit the voice of the turtledove. Blessed David speaks the same way in the psalm entitled "For the winepresses." Having said, "How lovely are your dwellings, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord; my heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God," he also adds the reason for the rejoicing, saying, "For the sparrow has found itself a house, and the turtledove a nest for herself, where she will lay her young." Then, to show what these are, he adds, "Your altars, Lord of hosts." He teaches us that the young birds are those who have received rebirth through the washing, and their nests are the divine altars, where they are nourished and fed, grow their feathers, and little by little attain perfection. Their mother, who bore them as it were, is the grace of the Holy Spirit, figuratively called a turtledove because the creature is chaste and loves solitude, and builds its nests in leafy trees. So the bridegroom says, "The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land, and the fig tree has put forth its early figs": that is, the early fruit of faith. Through it the other fruit, that of [?], also becomes lasting. It does not drop off but ripens and is made very sweet. "And the vines are in blossom; they have given forth their fragrance." The vines so called [?], he says, have blossomed and give forth their fragrance.

14. "Arise, then, come, my companion, into the shelter of the rock, next to the outer wall." He calls her into the shelter of the rock so that she may not become black again. By the rock he means the pious faith, the true confession. For when the Lord asked the disciples, "Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?" blessed Peter said, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." And he answered him, "Truly, truly I say to you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it." He also wants her to go outside the present life. That is why blessed Paul, writing to the Hebrews, says, "Let us go out to him, then, outside the camp, bearing his reproach." He wants her to look not at the things that are seen but at those that are not seen, "for the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal." That is why he urges her to come next to the outer wall, as if to say to her: "Put to death your members that are on the earth. Practise living as if without flesh while in the body. Show freedom from passion in the midst of passions. Go outside the present city and its walls. For if you do not come right up to the outer wall, you will not enjoy my fellowship. If you do not cry out with Paul, 'Though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh,' for no soldier entangles himself in the affairs of life, so that he may please the one who enlisted him; if you do not come to the borderland between the present and the things to come (for this, I think, is what the 'outer wall' indicates), our marriage will not take place. When you have come there, I urge you, show me your face. Your mind is pure, for none of life's cares obscures it. There I want to hear your voice, for there it too will be pure, freed from all licentiousness. Then your voice will be sweet to me and your face lovely, for I see my own beauty mirrored in you, and I hear a voice adorned with my words." Having said these things to the bride, the bridegroom gives orders to his own servants:

15. "Catch us the little foxes that ruin the vineyards." Some interpreters have taken "little" with the vineyards. It makes no difference whether the sense is this or that. He calls foxes those who have a crafty mind and ruin the Churches of the Lord, which have just begun to blossom. That is why he says, "And our vines are in blossom." By

the foxes he hints at the heretics who make war on the souls of the Church and try, treacherously and craftily, to steal away those who have not yet become firm in the faith. With persuasive words and the snares and tangles of their syllogisms they deceive the simpler sort, and so ruin the vines. For this reason he orders those who have received the gift of teaching to hunt and trap them with the refutations of the truth, and to free the blossoming vines from the harm they do. When the bride hears these words, she says at once: 16. "My beloved is mine, and I am his." "As he preferred me to all others, so I put him before all, and I will not consent to be joined to anyone else. I loathe those who bear both the name and the villainy of foxes." For it would be wrong for one who has been loved and counted worthy of so much not to repay the one who loved her in equal measure, as far as she can. Like this is what blessed Paul wrote to the Corinthians: "The body is not for fornication but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body." So too is his saying, "But whatever gains I had, these I have counted as loss for Christ's sake. Indeed, I count all things as refuse, so that I may gain Christ." So too is this: "I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me." So too this: "Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will affliction, or distress, or famine, or persecution, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?" and what follows. So too this: "But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world." To these the bride's words are alike: "My beloved is mine, and I am his." She also indicates who he is, what he is always doing, and where, and when, and until when. "He who pastures," she says, "among the lilies, (17) until the day breathes and the shadows move." We should note that the bridegroom first called himself a lily, speaking as a man: "I am the flower of the plain, the lily of the valleys." Second, he called the bride herself one: "As a lily among thorns, so is my companion among the daughters." And here he has called the pasture itself lilies: "He who pastures among the lilies." For the food offered to the sheep, he says, is full of fragrance. This is according to the Seventy. But Symmachus says, "Those who pasture flowers," so that clearly those who pasture are themselves

the flowers that he called lilies. "Until the day breathes and the shadows move." He calls human affairs shadows. That is why blessed David says, "Like a shadow as it declines I was taken away," and again, "My days pass away like a shadow." And the noble Job: "For the life of man on earth is a shadow." For nothing of the present life's seeming pleasures is lasting or secure, stable, enduring, or in any way substantial: not wealth, not glory, not power, not bodily health, not good looks, nor anything else of the kind. They are shadowy, and dissolve just as shadows do. So the bridegroom pastures us until the scorching heat of the day has passed and the dew of salvation breathes upon us, and the shadows move away, and the things to come appear, which have an enduring and lasting existence. And since the perfected souls betrothed to the bridegroom are as one to him, they answer him in the singular, saying, "My beloved is mine, and I am his": that is, "My beloved is seen by me according to the image, and I live for him and not for myself," as the great Apostle says. "He who pastures among the lilies": that is, he who by his holy commandments governs the rational sheep, namely those taught by them, through the souls of teachers that are not choked by the cares of life. "Until the day breathes and the shadows move": that is, until the day of the age to come arrives, all-radiant and without shadow, and all present things, since they are shadows of the things to come, pass away; the day on which the shepherd [...] his own flock
Verse 1. "On my bed at night I sought him whom my soul loved. I sought him and did not find him. I called him, and he did not answer

me. (2) I will rise and go around in the city, in the marketplaces and in the streets, and I will seek him whom my soul loved. I sought him and did not find him. I called him, and he did not answer me." The God of all often trains the souls of the pious by allowing them to fall into various trials. Sometimes he grants them deliverance when they ask, and sometimes he delays the gift, contriving benefit for his devotees from every side. Such is what David says: "How long, Lord, will you forget me? For ever? How long will you turn your face away from me? How long shall I take counsel in my soul, with sorrow in my heart day and night? How long shall my enemy be exalted over me?" For, as is likely, he had often prayed and asked for deliverance from his troubles without obtaining his request. So, distraught as one who had failed, and in anguish, he uses words like these. Blessed Paul also says, "So that I might not be too elated by the abundance of revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to buffet me, so that I might not be too elated. Three times I begged the Lord about this, and he said to me, 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.'" Paul begs and does not obtain, for not receiving what he asked was more beneficial. So, being taught what he did not know, he accepts with pleasure not receiving what he had asked for, and cries out, "Most gladly, then, will I rather boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell upon me." And Elijah, greatly terrified by Jezebel's threats, flees into the desert and seeks his helper. The wise trainer and judge of the contests of the pious leaves him for a little while to be exercised by fear, and then appears to him and, as if he did not know, asks the reason for his flight. He does not mock him, but teaches him the purpose of the flight, and trains him to be forgiving, since he is clothed in human nature and assailed by its passions. But it is time to return to our subject. Here the bride, the bridegroom having left her for a short while, looks for him on her bed, and that not by day but at night; yet she does not find him resting there. And she does this not only seeking him but also calling him. She gets up and roams the city, the marketplaces, the streets, for longing compelled her, and the flame of love did not allow her to stay at home. She also comes upon the guards of the city and asks them, saying: (3, 4) "The watchmen found me, those who go around in the city. 'Have you seen him whom my soul loved?' It was but a little while after I passed from them that I found him whom my soul loved." His beneficence in activity, and his immutability in essence.

"But why could I not find him who is beneficent and immutable in essence [?]? For even if, on this basis, I called him Good and Truth, he did not answer me, since he is beyond these too, for his name is above every name. So, as I said, I have not yet been able to find my beloved. But the holy angels found me, the watchmen, those who go around in the city. They found me while they were cleansing me through practice and enlightening me through contemplation: me, who had been lost through vice and ignorance, had once become a disciple of the spirits of wickedness, and for that reason was not found [fit] for discipleship to these good angels [?]. They keep watch over my visible and invisible movements, and every thought and deed, for praise or reproof on the fearful day of judgment. So, leaving none of these unexamined, they surround me, making their rounds in me as in a city. When they had come upon me in this way, I said to them, 'Have you seen him whom my soul loved?' That is: 'Him whom I longed to grasp but could not, have you at least, who dance around him as ministering spirits, seen what his nature is, so that you may teach me this too?' But since the bridegroom is incomprehensible in essence even to the holy angels, they gave me no answer to my question. By their silence they taught me that he is not comprehensible even to them: the uncreated is not comprehensible to creatures. So I passed on from them too, searching for the one I longed for. 'And it was but a little while after I passed from them that I found him whom my soul loved. I held him fast.' That is: since it is only created, I passed in mind beyond even the angelic nature itself as a short step, so as to find the uncreated one, my beloved. I held him, as my benefactor, by faith alone, having gone through all beings and been assured by experience itself that the cause of all is above all beings, and is seen in its essence in no nature, whether sensible or intelligible, since it is beyond essence. So I passed through all beings, seeking to bring my most longed-for bridegroom into my home. 'And I did not let him go until I brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her who conceived me.' That is: I did not stop seeking my lover until I had brought him into the mind. The mind is the house of the wisdom of God, who is the cause of all things as a mother is, since the mind is able to contain that wisdom by virtue of the likeness. And again it is her chamber, since by virtue of the image it holds her hidden treasures stored within itself. This wisdom conceived me, since before the foundation of the world she had her supremely good will toward me. For this reason, for my sake she brought into being human nature as a whole, and indeed the universe [?]." "On my bed at night I sought him whom my soul loved; I sought him and did not find him." And having passed these by a little, she says that she found him and did not

let him go until she had brought him into her mother's house, and into the chamber of her who conceived her. By the city he means the house of God, which we call the church; by the marketplaces and streets, the divine Scriptures; and by the guards of the city, the holy prophets and the sacred apostles, whom the pious soul questions in its longing for the divine Word. After them she finds the bridegroom escorted by certain guards or staff-bearers. She takes hold of him and holds him fast, and will not let him go until she has brought him into her mother's house, and into the chamber of her who conceived her. We know that the mother of the pious is the Jerusalem above, of which blessed Paul says, "But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is the mother of us all." So the bride, having taken hold of the bridegroom, promises not to leave him until they enter the bridal chamber and the inner room prepared for them [?]. Having told these things to the maidens, she again urges them to a like longing, and says: (5) "I have adjured you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and by the strengths of the field, that you do not rouse or awaken love until it pleases." This is clear from what was explained at the beginning of this discourse, for she lays this oath upon them twice, wishing to instil in them a warm love for the bridegroom. When the bride has said these things and has received an indescribable beauty from the bridegroom's embrace, the divine powers say in amazement: (6) "Who is this coming up from the desert like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the powders of the perfumer?" When they saw the bridegroom ascending into heaven after his victory over the devil and the destruction of death, they marvelled and said, "Who is this king of glory?" and learned that he is "the Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle." Then, wishing to learn more precisely, they asked again, "Who is this king of glory?" and heard that "the Lord of hosts, he is the king of glory." In the same way here, marvelling at the bride's loveliness, they say, "Who is this coming up from the desert?" They call human nature a desert because of its former ungodliness. That is why Isaiah says, "Rejoice, thirsty desert; let the desert rejoice and blossom like a lily." Just as here they are astonished that such beauty has sprung up from the desert, so in Isaiah's prophecy they marvel when they see the bridegroom, and say, "Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments red from Bozrah?" So too [?].

Edom signifies the earth, and Bozrah the flesh. And astonished at his beauty they cry out: "This one is beautiful in his apparel, with force and strength. Why are your garments red, as from a trodden winepress full of what has been trampled?" And they say: "Being in a body, he shines" [?]. They have called his body his apparel, and his beauty is forceful, compelling all who see it. So here too they are astonished, not only that the bride is beautiful, but that she is also coming up from the wilderness, that is, rising from the depth to the height, and making her way from lowly things to lofty ones. "And she is like," it says, "stems of smoke, perfumed." The construction is obscure; for the Seventy, keeping slavishly to the Hebrew tongue, did not make the sense clear; but Aquila and Symmachus have shown us the meaning by saying, "like smoke from incense." And the smoke of incense often imitates a stem, taking a kind of shape in the air. And fittingly they say that she resembles the smoke of incense, she who, according to blessed Paul, has presented her members as a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, and continually offers the sacrifice of praise, and has put to death her members that are on earth, and has been buried with Christ, and has brought herself to God as a whole burnt offering. They also teach what sort of incense smoke they likened her to: for they say, "myrrh and frankincense, from all the powders of the perfumer." It is clear that frankincense was assigned to God under the Mosaic law [?] … So by these names those who admire the bride's beauty signify that she is fragrant and likened to the vapour of incense for this reason: because she worships both the humanity and the divinity, and while believing in the death, she also confesses the existence before the ages. From all the powders of the perfumer, then, they admire her myrrh and frankincense. For she has the other virtues too, gathering them as from a kind of perfumer, the divine Scripture; but her special treasures are the myrrh and the frankincense, that is, theology and the economy. Thus, having admired the bride's beauty, they describe to her the wealth of the bridegroom, and say: (7, 8) "Behold the bed of Solomon; sixty mighty men are round about it, from the mighty men of Israel. All of them hold swords, trained in war; each man has his sword upon his thigh, because of fear in the nights." We must ask first of all why they call the bridegroom Solomon. "Solomon" means "peaceable"; and this can be found in Chronicles, for God says to David, when he wished to build the temple:

"Behold, a son is born to you; he shall be a man of rest, and I will give him rest from all his enemies round about, for Solomon is his name; and I will give peace and quiet to Israel in his days. He shall build a house for my name, and he shall be a son to me, and I will be a father to him, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom in Israel forever." But it is evident that Solomon died, having lived no very long time, and that his throne came to an end. So it is our peaceable Lord whom he calls Solomon, of whom blessed Paul says: "For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the dividing wall of the partition." That is why blessed David too entitles Psalm 71 "For Solomon," yet recounts in it the achievements of our Saviour. "For he shall judge," it says, "the poor of the people, and save the sons of the needy, and humble the false accuser; and he shall endure with the sun, and before the moon, for generations of generations." But Solomon neither endured with the sun nor was before the moon for generations of generations. These things rather fit Jesus Christ, who sprang from Solomon according to his humanity; who, existing before the ages, "came down like rain upon a fleece, and like drops falling upon the earth." Here he called the Virgin a fleece. For just as rain falls noiselessly upon a fleece, so that saving birth took place without any of mankind knowing it. To this he adds: "In his days righteousness shall spring up, and abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away. And he shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the inhabited world," and all that follows, which holds to the same sense; for now is not the time to interpret the psalm. It was not Solomon who ruled to the ends of the inhabited world, but Jesus Christ, who sprang from Solomon according to his human nature, and who is called Solomon because he is peaceable and gentle and the giver of peace. Now that we have learned who Solomon is, come, let us take up the interpretation. "Behold the bed of Solomon." Let us understand the bridegroom's bed as the divine Scriptures. For in them the bride, as it were reclining with the bridegroom and receiving the seeds of teaching, conceives, carries, travails and gives birth to spiritual benefit, so that she cries out with the prophet: "Because of the fear of you, Lord, we conceived in the womb, and travailed, and brought forth; we have wrought the spirit of your salvation upon the earth." "Sixty mighty men," it says, "are round about it, from the mighty men of Israel. All of them hold swords, trained in war; each man has his sword upon his

thigh, because of fear in the nights." I think the number sixty is set down here not for that particular quantity, but that by this term are meant the saints who distinguished themselves under the Old Covenant. For they say that ten is a perfect number, while six suits those under the law: "For six days," it says, "you shall work." So they say that those who were perfected under the law stand around the bed, tracing their descent from Israel, mighty beyond all others, holding swords, skilled in the experience of war, and carrying other swords upon their thighs. "Because of fear," it says, "in the nights." Symmachus made this clearer by saying, "because of terrors by night." These mighty men, it says, surround his bed, guarding the bride against the assaults of the adversaries. They carry two swords, one on the thigh and the other in the hand: the word of refutation, and the hidden, mystical word; the word of refutation ready at hand, the mystical word stored away within, in the sheath. (9, 10) "King Solomon made himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon. He made its pillars of silver, and its back of gold; its steps of purple; within it a pavement of stone: love from the daughters of Jerusalem." Here again let us understand the litter as the holy apostles, who carried the name of the Lord before nations and kings and the sons of Israel. For Christ says this to Ananias about blessed Paul: "Go, for this man is a chosen vessel of mine, to carry my name before nations and kings and the sons of Israel." And the inspired Paul himself cries out: "Since you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me." Blessed Habakkuk also calls them horses: "For you shall mount," he says, "upon your horses, and your riding is salvation." And again: "You made your horses ride into the sea, stirring up many waters." He calls the nations the sea, which was thrown into turmoil when the apostles preached; that is why the unbelievers said of them: "These men who have turned the world upside down have come here too, and Jason has received them." Those whom Habakkuk named horses, then, we find called a litter in the Song of Songs. "King Solomon made himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon." The divine Scripture often calls Jerusalem and the multitude of the Jews "Lebanon"; and we demonstrated this from the prophetic writings in the introduction to this work. Since, then, the blessed apostles traced their descent from them,

it fittingly says that the litter was built of the wood of Lebanon. "He made its pillars," it says, "of silver." And we find them also named pillars, for blessed Paul, writing to the Galatians, says: "Peter and James and John, who were reputed to be pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcision." They say also that its back is of gold. This signifies the proclamation of the gospel, on which the divine Word rests. "Its steps of purple": for to those who are beginning it is fitting to be ruled as by a king, but to those who are perfected, to be led as a bride [?]. "And within it a pavement of stone": for the divine oracles are like pearls and precious stones, as the prophet said: "The judgments of the Lord are true, justified altogether, more to be desired than gold and much precious stone." And again: "Behold, I have longed for your commandments more than gold and topaz." And, according to the Lord's word, "The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls." And elsewhere he says: "Do not cast your pearls before swine." Having shown that the king's litter is of this kind, they urge the daughters of Jerusalem to go out to behold the bridegroom and to see the crown set before him, and they say: (11) "Go out and see King Solomon, daughters of Zion, in the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, and on the day of the gladness of his heart." What they mean, to give the interpretation briefly and clearly and avoid length, is this: "O daughters of Jerusalem" and "Zion" — and blessed Paul taught us that Zion is the heavenly one, saying: "But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels in festal gathering, and to the church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven." "You then," they say, "O daughters of Zion and Jerusalem, go out and see; for it is impossible for us to see unless we get outside the affairs of this life. Behold the king crowned with love. For he so loved the world that, being in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. He so loved the world that he was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb dumb before its shearer; and he redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. That is why he says: 'Greater love than this no one can show, that someone lay down his life for his friends.'" Thus, then, his mother crowned him. By his mother he means Judea, according to his humanity, who

gave him this crown unwillingly. For she crowned him with thorns, to dishonour him; but through the thorns he received the crown of love. For he bore the dishonour willingly and went to his passion of his own accord; that is why he called that day the day of his wedding and the day of the gladness of his heart. For on that day the communion of the marriage took place. "For after supper," it says, "he took bread, and having given thanks he broke it and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take, eat of it, all of you; for this is my body, which is broken for you for the forgiveness of sins; do this in remembrance of me." Those, then, who eat the members of the bridegroom and drink his blood come to share in the communion of his marriage. For this reason the bridegroom's attendants urge the daughters of Zion and Jerusalem: "Go out and see the crown of his love, with which Judea, who bore him, adorned him against her will, and crowned him on the day of his wedding." When they have spoken thus, the bridegroom again converses with the bride and says:

(1) "Behold, you are beautiful, my companion; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves, apart from your silence." Astonished at her beauty, he says a second time: "Behold, you are beautiful." Then he describes her loveliness feature by feature. He calls her eyes doves, praising their spiritual contemplation, and because they do not gape after the things of sense but seek the things above, "where Christ is," according to Paul, "seated at the right hand of God." He also admires her well-timed silence. For we find this praised among the men of old as well; that is why we hear in the Psalms: "I set a guard on my mouth when the sinner stood against me." And in our singing we say: "Set a guard, Lord, on my mouth, and a door to enclose my lips." And we find the Lord, according to the prophecy of Isaiah, not opening his mouth in his humiliation, and, according to the Gospel narrative, being questioned by Pilate and not answering. So the bridegroom praises the bride's well-timed silence, since he too made use of it at the proper time. He praises her hair as well; he admires also her teeth:

"Your hair is like flocks of goats, which have been revealed from Gilead. (2) Your teeth are like flocks of shorn ewes, which have come up from the washing, all of them bearing twins, and none among them is barren." Yet we must not understand the hair as hair [?]

nor the teeth as teeth. Rather, by the hair is meant what is, as it were, superfluous and bodily in the bride; for hair is dead and without sensation. What he indicates is this: "Even in those matters in which you must of necessity engage in human affairs, you have what is praiseworthy and seemly, and you resemble the flock of goats grazing on Mount Gilead and made conspicuous by the height of the mountain." Of this mountain the prophet Jeremiah says: "Is there no balm in Gilead, or is there no physician there?" And we should consider whether by the flock of goats the text is here hinting at those who come from sin to repentance and therefore graze on Mount Gilead in order to obtain healing remedies and cure, and whether it indicates that the humble parts of the bride, her lowest members, those that are as it were dead and insensible, are compared to the good deeds of that flock. "And your teeth are such: clean, and free of all superfluous talk, of coarse jesting and foolish talk, of lying and obscene speech, so that they resemble the flocks of shorn ewes, which have put off what is superfluous, which have come up from the washing." I think that by the flocks of shorn ewes the bridegroom indicates those who have shorn off sin through baptism and have been cleansed "by the washing of water with the word," as blessed Paul says. For thus, he says, you have continued to keep your teeth clean and free from the filth of wicked words, so that you resemble those who have just been granted saving baptism. "And those flocks all bear twins, and none among them is barren": for I do not liken you to those who after saving baptism run back to wickedness, but to those who guard the gift given them and bring forth the twofold virtue, that of contemplation and that of action. Having thus praised these features of the bride, he goes on to the rest and says: (3) "Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your speech is lovely." By the scarlet thread he reminds her of Rahab the harlot, who fulfilled the type of her in the Old Testament. For she received the spies sent by Joshua son of Nun, and through them became worthy of eternal life; and she received as a sign of [?] the scarlet thread. She was commanded to let it down through the window, so that when the Israelites entered the city, the sign, once seen, would deliver her from those who were slaying, and secure her salvation. This sign the bridegroom sees on the bride's mouth, as though placed in the window, and he says: "Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your speech is lovely." For your mouth has received the dye of my blood, and brings forth words of truth which, as with a kind of thread, catch the hearers like fish

and bind them fast. For your lovely speech enchants and charms them, and does not let them go away, but compels them to wait upon your lips. He praises also her cheek: "For like the rind of a pomegranate," he says, "is your cheek, apart from your silence." This signifies the blush of modesty that arises in her; because of it she also keeps silence at the proper time, concealing at the proper time the more mystical words, as the rind of the pomegranate conceals its seeds. (4) "Your neck is like the tower of David, built for Thalpioth. A thousand shields hang upon it, all the darts of the mighty." Aquila rendered "Thalpioth" as "battlements," and Symmachus as "heights." Just as, he says, the tower built by David rises above the battlements on which it is built, and is lofty and conspicuous, so your neck is lofty and raised on high, gazing about at the things above, ranging among the things above. For it does not gape toward the earth like the irrational beasts, nor does it bend toward the belly in imitation of swine, but it is lifted up and raised on high, bearing a thousand shields and all the darts of the mighty. The number is set down not for a definite quantity but for a multitude. For your neck, which bears your head and your mouth, holds all the teachings of the others, figuratively called darts, with which you overcome all your adversaries. It also has many shields, with which you fence yourself about and quench the fiery darts of the evil one; for you are clothed in the full armour of the Spirit. And you easily wound those who oppose you, since you have all the darts of the mighty, refuting them now through the prophets, now through the apostles, and laying bare their weakness. (5, 6) "Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle, that feed among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows move." We understand these words too in keeping with what has been said; and again we take the breasts to be the fountains of teaching, offered suitably to each stage of life, giving milk to some and supplying solid food to others. That is why he likens them to the fawns of a gazelle, admiring their keen sight and their power of contemplation. He says "fawns of a gazelle" because, according to blessed Paul, "Now we know in part, but then we shall know fully, even as we have been fully known." And since now we know in part and prophesy in part, the breasts of teaching are called fawns of a gazelle; "but when the perfect comes, then what is in part will be done away." And he says that these feed among the lilies,

that is, they partake of fragrant pasture; and this is the teaching of the Spirit. According to Symmachus, it says "pasturing flowers"; for the bride's breasts pasture and shepherd those who have been counted worthy to become a flower of the Spirit, offering them the streams of teaching "until the day breathes," and the scorching heat ceases, that is, this toilsome life, "and the shadows move," that is, present things, which are likened to shadows, as was said before. Having thus praised the bride's members, he says: "I will go my way to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense." Since, he says, you are so comely, so lovely, so radiant in beauty, so wounded with love for me, I accept death on your behalf, and I will go my way to the mountain of myrrh; but I will rise again and return to the hill of frankincense. We have already said that by myrrh he indicates death, and by frankincense the divine nature. We must ask, then, why he has put "mountain" for death but "hill" for the divinity. It is because it is a great and ineffable thing, beyond the reach of human thought, that he who was in the form of God, not counting equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptying himself and taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man, should humble himself unto death, even death on a cross. But to return to his own glory and to be glorified with the glory he had before the world came to be was nothing great or laborious, but very easy indeed. That is why he says "mountain" of myrrh but "hill" of frankincense, showing that the latter is effortless for him and very easy, while the former is steep because of his human nature. That is also why, when he came to the passion itself, he says: "Now my soul is troubled"; and, "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me." But again he adds: "And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour? But for this very reason I have come to this hour." Pointing to this here as well, he says: "I will go my way to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense." For I do both willingly, not forced or compelled by anyone: "For I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again. No one takes it from me; I lay it down of myself, that I may take it up again." (7) "You are all beautiful, my companion, all beautiful, and there is no blemish in you." These words resemble those of blessed Paul, for he too says of the bridegroom: "that he might present the Church to himself in glory, having no spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she might be holy and without blemish." Without blemish

…but she became beautiful as well, once she had come near the bridegroom and received the radiance that shines from him, and had become full of light from that light. May it be granted to us, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face as in a mirror, to be transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Lord who is the Spirit. With him be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

[?]… so that our eyes may become doves, seeing spiritually, passing beyond the veil of the letter and clearly bringing out the hidden mysteries. For there is no other way to learn the meaning of divine Scripture, and especially of the Song of Songs, unless the one who inspired its writers himself enlightens our power of sight, sending rays of grace, and shows us the hidden sense. Come then: let us call on him who reveals mysteries, as the wise Daniel puts it, as our helper, and take up the interpretation of the book, keeping to its order. At the end of the preceding book we heard the bridegroom admiring the bride's beauty and

offering praise to each of her parts, and after that praising her as wholly blameless. For the choir of souls made perfect in virtue has no spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind, as blessed Paul says. Here he calls her from Lebanon, addressing her as bride, and says: "8. Come from Lebanon, bride, come from Lebanon. You will come and pass through from the beginning of faith, from the top of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards." These words seem to me to resemble what is said to the bride in Psalm 44: "Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father's house, and the king will desire

your beauty, for he is your Lord." There too the Word offers her advice and counsel, urging her to forget her people and her father's house, since otherwise the king would not desire her beauty. By "her people" and "her father's house" he means her old ways of life, of which blessed Paul says: "For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, hating one another. But when the goodness and loving-kindness of God our Saviour appeared, he saved us, not by works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his great mercy, through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, which he poured out on us richly," and so on. In this book, however, he calls her from Lebanon and from Senir. By Lebanon he signifies idolatry; by Senir, which means "the way of lamps," the way of life under [?the law]. For the law is a lamp, shining in the night, whereas Christ is the sun, shining as in daytime. That is why God says through the prophet: "But for those who fear me the sun of righteousness will rise, with healing in its wings." He adds Mount Hermon as well, and by it too he points to the law. For the great David says in the Psalms: "Like the dew of Hermon that comes down on the mountains of Zion"—that is, the teachings of the law, supplied to the mountains of Zion. By mountains we should understand those perfect in virtue, as lofty and conspicuous, and raised high in godly thought. So the bridegroom calls some from Lebanon, as people taught to wait upon idols, and others from Senir and Hermon, as people who receive the dew of the law and are enlightened by the divine commandments. To these he adds: "from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards." By the dens of lions he means the most insolent and frenzied of the Jews; by leopards the wise men of the Greeks, who cloaked their falsehood in the many colours of their words and the artifice of their sophistries, and so made it look plausible to the foolish. Having called the bride in this way, gathered her from the various mountains, secured her salvation through faith, and seen the beauty she gained from it, he says to her: "9. You have ravished our heart, my sister, my bride; you have ravished our heart with one of your eyes, with one ornament of your neck." For "you have ravished our heart" Symmachus has "you have emboldened us." What he means is something like this: "Your two eyes are wonderful and spiritual, and rightly called doves;

but one of them overwhelms me with amazement—the one that gazes on divine things, that has been taught to speak of God, that sees the hidden mysteries. And I admire all the ornaments of your neck"—by these he hints at practical virtue, since the neck bears the yoke of the divine commandments and draws and cuts the furrows of righteousness—"so I praise the other ornaments of virtue that shine on your neck, but I admire and marvel above all at the one; and struck by the beauty of that one necklace, and of the eye that contemplates divine things, I have been wounded with love for you." Let us ask, then, what that one ornament is which lies around her neck and surpasses the others, and let us learn from blessed Paul: "Faith, hope and love abide, these three; but the greatest of all of these is love." And again: "Love is the fulfilment of the law." And elsewhere: "The whole law and the prophets hang on this: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbour as yourself." It is this necklace of the bride, then, that the bridegroom admires—for Symmachus has "necklace" instead of "ornament." He also admires her one eye, not by way of disparaging the other, for he has already praised both, but because he knows that the contemplation of spiritual realities is more wonderful than the perception of things that are seen. "You have ravished our heart" means "you have stirred us to love and longing for you, having such an eye and wearing such a necklace." "10. How beautiful your breasts have become, my sister, my bride! How beautiful your breasts have become from wine! And the fragrance of your garments is beyond all spices." For from the spiritual wine and the mystical drink your breasts have gained greater loveliness. We have already said that the breasts are the fountains of teaching. And the fragrance of your garments is full of every grace and has become sweeter than all spices; for you have put on me, the bridegroom. Isaiah is witness to this, foretelling it and saying: "Let my soul rejoice in the Lord, for he has clothed me with the garment of salvation and put on me the tunic of gladness." These garments of yours give off so sweet a scent that the fragrance spreading everywhere from them surpasses the virtue of the law, which is figuratively called spices. He calls her not only bride but also sister, since blessed Paul too says: "so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers." And the Lord himself, when he had risen, said to the women standing by the tomb: "Go and

tell my brothers" and Peter: "See, he is going ahead of you into Galilee." So she is his sister, his bride and his neighbour. His neighbour, in the sense of "My soul has clung close behind you"; his bride, because she receives from him the seeds of teaching and bears the fruit of godliness; his sister, because she shares the same nature with him as regards his humanity. He goes on, then, recounting her praises, and says: "11. Your lips drip a honeycomb, bride; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense." Here we must set alongside these words the apostle's teaching, which says: "For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slaves or free, and we were all made to drink of one Spirit. For the body does not consist of one member but of many." And a little later: "If all were a single member, where would the body be?" And again: "Now you are the body of Christ, and individually members of it." So the Church, made up of many members, forms one body. Let us understand, then, that some in her are eyes, some ears, some lips. That is why the bridegroom says to her: "Your lips drip a honeycomb, bride; honey and milk are under your tongue." Here he means the teachers of the Church, who offer godly teaching, carrying as it were a honeycomb on their lips and letting the honey fall in drops. They have not only honey but also milk, and they offer each person the food that suits him—to infants what fits them, and to the perfect what is proper to them. The honeycombs carried on the teachers' lips are the divine Scriptures, and the bees that molded the wax and made the honey are the holy prophets and apostles. For they flew about the meadows of the all-holy Spirit, built for us, so to speak, the honeycombs of the divine Scriptures, filled them with the honey of teaching, and passed on the benefit to us. The letter is like the wax, and the meaning hidden in it like the honey; and the lips of godly teachers let fall drops of this honey. They also hold out milk, flowing from their tongue, to those who need milk. Then he again lingers in admiration of the bride's garments, and says: "And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense." We have already said that the bridegroom himself became her garment, and blessed Paul is witness, saying: "As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ." Now the bridegroom is both

God before the ages and man, born in the last days of the holy Virgin. Remaining what he was, he took on what is ours, and clothed the bride who had long been naked. That is why he says to her: "The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense"; for she has put on Christ, who is God and man, and frankincense is a symbol of speaking about God, since under the old law it was offered to God. "12. A garden locked, my sister, my bride, a garden locked, a fountain sealed." He calls her a garden because she bears not one fruit of godliness and virtue but many and varied ones; and locked, as being fenced about and safe from attack. For, he says, "the gates of Hades will not prevail against her." She is not like that vine transplanted out of Egypt, "which all who pass along the road have plucked; the boar from the forest has ravaged it, and the wild beast has fed on it." No, she is fenced and walled, and resembles a locked garden, which has many fruits of every kind but does not admit thieves and escapes the hands of those who plot against it. And she is a sealed fountain, for these streams are not poured out for all but for the worthy. Of this fountain the Lord says in the Gospels: "Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst again, but it will become in him a spring of living water welling up to eternal life." So he rightly calls her a sealed fountain, as one set before the worthy and not before all. For the divine mysteries are set before those who have been initiated, not the uninitiated; not before those who wallow in lawlessness after their initiation, but before those who live strictly, or are being cleansed through repentance. And he says not only "a garden locked and a fountain sealed," but also: "13–15. Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates, with the fruit of fruit trees, henna with nard; nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all the trees of Lebanon; myrrh and aloes, with all the finest perfumes; a fountain of gardens, a well of living water, rushing down from Lebanon." All these things, he says, you have sent me and offered me at the time of the wedding. First, the paradise of pomegranates, which was not without the other fruit trees either. I take the pomegranate to stand figuratively for love, since under one rind countless seeds lie packed together and joined to one another, yet do not crush or spoil one another, remaining sound unless some rot arises among them. From the partitions inside it one can also draw another interpretation. For among those who are being saved we see many orders: one order of those living in virginity, another of those practising continence, another

of those who bear the yoke of marriage; one of those who abound in wealth, another of those who live with poverty; one of slaves who love godliness, another of masters who exercise their authority lawfully. So the Church too has walls of division, as it were, separating the seeds into groups. That is why he likens the bride's shoots to a paradise of pomegranates. For first he admires her fruit of love, and then he says that she is rich in the other kinds of virtue as well: "with the fruit of fruit trees." Then he goes through them one by one: "henna with nard." Henna is a kind of tree from which a warming oil is made; nard is a fragrant spice, from which an oil of the same name is likewise made, also warming and useful for healing the body. He says too that the paradise has saffron. For we need not only things that warm us and kindle in us love for God, but also things that cool our unruly desires; and saffron is a cooling plant. "And calamus," he says, "and cinnamon." These too are kinds of spices, but they are to be understood figuratively. By the calamus, or reed, he means godly writings: "My tongue is the reed of a swift scribe." The aromatic reed is fragrant, and indeed the tongue of teachers of godliness is full of every sweet scent. Joined to the reed is cinnamon, which was offered to God under the old law, so that we may learn that writings about God are praiseworthy and fragrant, and comparable to the spices already mentioned. To these he adds: "with all the trees of Lebanon." For she has, he says, the virtue practised under the law too—not the virtue according to the letter, but that according to the spirit; for we have often been taught that Lebanon signifies Jerusalem. She also has "myrrh and aloes, with all the finest perfumes"—that is, the deadening of the passions, since myrrh belongs to the dead, and the bitterness of trials, since aloes are bitter. In a word, she has all the first among perfumes—not the second or the third, but the first, for the perfect have what is perfect. She also has "a fountain, and a well of living water, rushing down from Lebanon." For she has not only the teaching of the Gospel, flowing openly, but also the well of the law, which is a well of living water: its streams are hidden, yet they rush and make a sound, pouring down from Lebanon. For the life under the law flourished in Jerusalem, which is figuratively called Lebanon. But this well too passed over to the Lord's bride, the Church, and it is no longer hidden but rushes along and waters the paradise of the Church. Having heard the praises above, the bride, delighted and glad[?]…

…"my wine with my milk." For he does not reject the infants—those still at the breast, so to speak, and fed on milk—but accepts from them too the fruit proportionate to them. And being good, he also invites his friends to the feast, saying: "Eat, my neighbours, and drink, and be drunk, my kinsmen." Those who have been made perfect draw near to him, and those who keep the image incorrupt boast of their kinship with him. He urges them not only to drink but also to be drunk. For there is a drunkenness that produces sobriety, not madness; that does not weaken the limbs but strengthens them. "For your intoxicating cup, how excellent it is!" And elsewhere blessed David says again: "They will be drunk with the richness of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight." After these words from above, the bride says: "2. I sleep, but my heart is awake." For even if I am compelled by nature to close my eyes and accept sleep, in my mind I am awake, and I do not admit the sleep of sloth, as I await the bridegroom's coming. That is why I also hear his knocking. "For the voice of my kinsman," she says, "knocks at the door." Let us, if you will, set beside these words what the good shepherd says in the divine Gospels: "My sheep hear my voice." And again: "They will not follow a stranger, for they do not know the voice of strangers." Blessed, then, is the one who is shepherded and recognizes the shepherd's voice. Blessed is the one being adorned as a bride, who knows how to distinguish the voice of the adulterer from that of the bridegroom. Blessed is the one who says: "I will not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids," but stays awake and waits for the bridegroom, according to the Lord's own exhortation: "Keep awake," he says, "for you do not know at what hour your Lord is coming." Blessed Paul too offers this counsel, saying: "Keep awake, stand firm in the faith, be courageous, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love." So the bride, being awake even while she sleeps the sleep of the body, enjoys the bridegroom's voice and hears his knocking at the door. And what are the doors of the soul but the senses of the body, through which the bride admits the bridegroom, who not only knocks but also asks that the door be opened to him? "Open to me," he says, "my sister, my neighbour, my dove, my perfect one, for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night." By the night he means the uprising of the Jews against him, which took place at night; by the dew and the drops, the three days'

death, which the locks of his head underwent, and not he himself. Since, then, he says, I accepted death for your sake, and endured these things because of you, open to me and receive me. For I love your spiritual beauty and your perfection in virtue. That is why I call you my sister, my neighbour, my dove and my perfect one. My perfect one, because you fulfil the perfection I laid down as law; for I said: "Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect." And again: "If you wish to be perfect, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and take up your cross and follow me." I call you my dove, because you have become spiritual, have stripped off the old self with its passions and desires, and are able to see spiritually. My neighbour, because you walk in my footsteps and long to draw near to me; for I said: "Draw near to me, and I will draw near to you." And I call you my sister, not only because of our kinship in the nature I took on, but also because of our closeness in godliness. Hearing these words from above, the bride answers:

"3. I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?" From this we learn how much harm sloth brings, and how much toil it causes those who give in to it. For the bride, having put things off and being unwilling to open the door to the bridegroom at once, is forced a little later not only to walk as far as the door but to run into the city, wander about the marketplaces, and fall in with certain watchmen, from whom she even receives wounds; and only with difficulty does she find the bridegroom she longs for. Had she obeyed him at once when he called, she would have been spared all these troubles. As it is, she says: "I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?" Yet this is not what the bridegroom urges on her. He does not want her, once she has stripped off the old self, to put it on again; nor does he want her, once she has washed her feet and enjoyed the touch of his holy hands, to soil them again. He wants her to open to him, without toil and without defilement, the door either of hearing or of sight, so that the bridegroom may enter through knowledge or through hearing and dwell in sanctified souls. And since she was putting things off with those excuses, the bridegroom rouses her in another way, no longer only knocking from outside but also putting his hand in through an opening. By the hand we understand the sense of touch, and his divine working, which he made her feel, so that she cried out: "4–6. My kinsman put his hand in through the opening, and my belly was stirred for him. I rose to open to my kinsman;"

"My hands dripped myrrh, my fingers were full of myrrh, on the handles of the bolt. I opened to my beloved; my beloved had passed by. My soul went out at his word. I sought him, and did not find him; I called him, and he did not answer me. The watchmen who go about in the city found me; they struck me, they wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took my veil from me." Since she would not open at once to the one who knocked, he touches her through one of the senses, which she called a "hole," putting in his hand, that is, his power at work. He warms her and kindles her love; this is what "My belly was stirred for him" indicates, which Theodotion rendered "was warmed." And she rises, drunk with longing, runs to the door, and says: "My hands, holding the bolt and wanting to open it, dripped myrrh, and my fingers were full of myrrh. I am clothed in a complete mortification, down to my very extremities. But when I opened the door, I saw my beloved passing me by and not willing to come in. Yet I, bound to him by love and hanging on his sacred words, kept up the search, and went on crying out and calling him without ceasing. But he did not answer, nor did he think me worthy of a reply. As I wandered about, seeking the one I longed for, I fell in with those who live in the city and guard it. Not only did they mistreat me or scourge me; they also wounded me and took away my veil." By "watchmen of the walls" and "watchmen of the city" I think the bride means the demagogues, rulers and tyrants who long ago made war on the bride of God. They struck and wounded the triumphant martyrs, handed them over to death, stripped their souls, and took the body from the souls like a veil. For those martyrs, longing for the bridegroom and always proclaiming him in cities, in the countryside and in the remotest places, endured all these things. From what has been said, then, we are taught to put aside all hesitation and to open at once to the bridegroom when he knocks. Otherwise, once he has gone away, we will be forced to wander everywhere and search for the one we long for. "[?] by the powers and by the forces of the field: if you find my beloved, tell him that I am wounded by love." The bridegroom often appears even to those who are still imperfect and childlike, stooping to their weakness and urging them toward perfection: "For those who are strong have no need of a physician, but those who are sick." She adjures [?]. [Apparatus notes: "fingers": the manuscript prefixes "the"; "myrrh full"; "nodding, he passed by"; "(if) you tell him."]

So she adjures the maidens, if they should find her beloved, to tell him how great a love she has for him, and that she has been wounded by the chosen arrow of love. The maidens do not know the beloved's name, for they are still imperfect and do not know the depth of the mysteries.

9. "What is your beloved more than another beloved, O fairest among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have adjured us so?" "For we have often heard you saying, 'my beloved,' 'of my beloved,'" they say, "and we do not know the meaning of what you are saying. Since an oath now stands between us, we cannot pass over your commands in silence. So teach us, O fairest among women, for you are more comely than all of them, maidens and concubines alike: what does this name mean to you? You are always bringing it up, saying now 'of my beloved,' now 'my beloved.' If we learn from you who he is and what marks he bears, we will serve you and carry out your command." So the bride teaches those who are her pupils the marks of the bridegroom, and says to them: 10–16. "My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of ten thousands. His head is gold of Uphaz; his locks are palm fronds, black as a raven. His eyes are like doves by brimming waters, washed in milk, sitting by brimming waters. His cheeks are like bowls of spice, putting forth perfumes; his lips are lilies dripping with abundant myrrh. His hands are finely turned, golden, filled with gold of Tarshish; his belly is an ivory tablet upon a sapphire stone. His legs are marble pillars, set upon golden bases; his appearance is like choice frankincense, like cedars. His throat is sweetness, and he is wholly desire.
