This is my beloved, and this is my companion, O daughters of Jerusalem." When the maidens ask, the bride teaches them the marks of the beloved and says: "My beloved is white and ruddy." She puts "white" first and "ruddy" second. For he was always God, but he also became man. He did not abandon what he was, nor was he changed into a man; he put on human nature. So he is white as God, for what is brighter than light? And he is the true light, as the Gospels say: "For there was," it says,

"the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world." And he is not only white [?] but also ruddy; for he is not only God [?] but also man. Ruddiness signifies what is earthly. That is why in Isaiah the divine powers ask, when they see him ascending from earth to heaven [?], and say: "Who is this who comes from Edom, [?] the redness of his garments from Bozrah? This one is beautiful in his robe, with force and with strength." And they marvel at his [?] beauty in the body, calling this his robe. "For he is fair in beauty beyond the

"the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world." And he is not only white [?] but also ruddy; for he is not only God but also man. Ruddiness signifies what is earthly. That is why in Isaiah the divine powers ask, when they see him ascending from earth to heaven, and say: "Who is this who comes from Edom, the redness of his garments from Bozrah? This one is beautiful in his robe, with force and with strength." They marvel at his beauty in the body as well, calling it his robe. "For he is fair in beauty beyond the sons of men" as man; his divine beauty cannot be compared with anything, since it is beyond reach. And they ask him, saying: "Why are your garments red, as from a trodden winepress, full of what has been trampled down?" Since they long to learn the cause of the redness, he teaches them and says: "I trod the winepress all alone, and of the nations there was no one with me." For it was neither an envoy nor an angel, but the Lord himself who saved us, as Isaiah prophesied. "And I trampled them," he says, "in my fury, and crushed them in my wrath." He means the demons hostile to human nature and their army. "And my garments were spattered with their defeat": in conquering them and destroying their power, he received some drops of blood on his garments. This signifies the three-day death. One must note carefully that he does not say "I was spattered," but "my garments were spattered with their defeat," that is, my body. For the divine nature is impassible, but the body underwent the suffering. God the Word was united with it [?], yet drew no suffering from it, since the Divine is by nature above suffering. That is why the bride says: "My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of ten thousands." For the firstfruits is superior to all nature: "He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth." Therefore he was offered as a spotless sacrifice for the whole race. For this reason too the God of all foretells through Isaiah the prophet, saying: "Behold my servant, whom I have chosen, my chosen one, in whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations." Fittingly, then, the bride says: "My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of ten thousands." Our sins were red as purple and as scarlet, so it was fitting that he who took them up should become ruddy and be called so. "And his head," she says, "is gold of Uphaz." Symmachus has "like a precious stone," and the fifth edition has "marked with gold." By his head she figuratively means the Divinity, which was called white [?]. [?]

I take the graces poured out from his head to be called locks. In one respect they are called black, in another palm fronds. For palm fronds are the fruit of the male palms; they are laid on the female trees and make their fruit ripen. Those who believe in him enjoy his varied gifts and so bear him the fruit of godliness. Fittingly, then, she likens his locks to palm fronds. She calls them black because the deep, dark colour shows that his dispensations are beyond reach. "Locks, palm fronds, black as a raven": she has brought in the raven here only for its colour. "His eyes," she says, "are like doves by brimming waters." Here again, through his eyes, she marvels at his power of sight. So she says they are like doves by brimming waters, and she reminds us of the dove that came down upon him at the Jordan. And let no one be surprised that it says "like doves" rather than "dove." For we find divine Scripture speaking not only of "spirit" but also of "spirits." This is not because there are many Holy Spirits, for there is one Holy Spirit, the Paraclete. Rather, blessed Paul is accustomed to call his gifts spirits: "For the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets." Christ the Master had all the gifts of the Spirit in his humanity, and so the bride says: "His eyes are like doves by brimming waters." His eyes look continually to the bounty of baptism, waiting for those who are being saved and longing for the salvation of all. And the doves, she says, are "washed in milk, and sitting by brimming waters." Some they nourish with milk, those who need this food. Others, who have grown old through sin, they make new and renew, "sitting by brimming waters" and sanctifying them. She rightly said "brimming waters." For it does not receive those whose faith is imperfect and who do not come with sincere faith. Such was Simon, who was indeed baptized, but unworthy [?] [1 Cor. 14:32]

1. "My beloved has gone down into his garden, to the bowls of spice, to pasture his flock in the gardens and to gather lilies." We should ask why he speaks of one garden and also of many: "He went down into his garden," and "to pasture in the gardens." The Church is indeed one, as blessed Paul says: "For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ." And again: "Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the Church." Yet blessed Paul also calls the churches many. He does this because they are divided by place, not in spirit: "Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through men … to the churches of Galatia." And writing to the Corinthians he says: "Let your women keep silent in the churches." That is why the bride says: "My beloved has gone down into his garden, to the bowls of spice, to pasture in the gardens and to gather lilies." For he shepherds all the churches. He delights in the bowls of spice, that is, in those who have taken on his fragrance. He gathers those who have imitated the bride's beauty and have become lilies, and he joins them to the bride. To this the bride adds: 2. "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine; he pastures his flock among the lilies." For I cling to him and have entrusted myself to him. He has honored me above the whole world and joined me to himself. When I had grown old he renewed me, when I was poor he made me rich, when I was ugly he made me lovely, and when I had festering, foul-smelling wounds he healed them and filled me with fragrance. That is why I say: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine; he pastures his flock among the lilies," or, in Symmachus's version, "he who pastures the flowers." For he shepherds those who have become lilies, and he pastures the worthy among lilies. And nothing is more fragrant than the divine Scriptures. The bridegroom heard the bride's words. He took pity on her as she longed for him, picturing him night and day, talking about him and describing his beauty. So he appears to her and says: 3. "You are beautiful, my close one, like good pleasure, lovely as Jerusalem, awe-inspiring as ordered ranks." He names her after the thing that came about for her sake. "For since the Lord took pleasure in his land, and turned back the captivity of Jacob, and forgave his people's iniquities, and covered all

their sins," it is fitting that he calls her "good pleasure." Earlier she named him "desire," taking the name from her own feeling: because she desires him continually, she calls him desire. In the same way he, having taken pleasure in her and wishing to betroth her and join her to himself, names her "good pleasure." For this is how you are beautiful, he says: as one in whom I have taken pleasure and whom I have loved. You are not only beautiful but lovely, and not just lovely, but lovely "as Jerusalem." He does not mean the Jerusalem below but the one above, of which blessed Paul says: "But the Jerusalem above is free; she is the mother of us all." You resemble her, my close one, for you have imitated the angelic way of life. On earth you practice in advance the things of heaven. Though you walk in the flesh, you do not wage war according to the flesh. You press on toward the goal, for the prize of the upward call, and you seek the things above, where I am seated at the right hand of God. That is why you are "lovely as Jerusalem." And you are not just lovely: you fill those who see you with awe. Those who look on your order are astonished, for nothing in you is disordered, nothing undefined, nothing confused. Everything is ordered and clearly distinguished. You know exactly the proper order of things: you have been taught to honor the bridegroom above all, and after him those who are close to him. To this he adds: 4. "Turn your eyes away from me, for they have set me on wing." What he means is this: the beauty of your eyes, the contemplation of your [?] sight, and the keenness of your mind have drawn me into love for you. But do not gaze at me beyond due measure, or you will bring harm on yourself. For I am beyond reach and beyond comprehension. I surpass every grasp, not only human but angelic. If you try to overstep the limits and pry into what lies beyond your power, you will not only find nothing but will also dim your eye and make it duller. Such is the nature of light: it illuminates the eye, but it punishes the eye's greed by harming it. "Turn your eyes away from me," then. "Do not search out what is too hard for you, and do not seek what is too strong for you; think about what has been commanded you." To this he adds the earlier praises once more, saying: 5–6. "Your hair is like flocks of goats that have appeared from Gilead. Your teeth are like flocks of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing; all of them bear twins, and none among them is barren. Like a scarlet thread

are your lips, and your speech is lovely." 6. "Like the rind of a pomegranate is your cheek, apart from your silence." We have interpreted these words above and think it unnecessary to interpret them twice. Anyone who has forgotten the interpretation can go back to it and find the meaning. It was not idly or at random that he offered the same praises to the bride twice. He was reminding her of her own beauty and urging her to keep it intact and let no blemish touch it. "See," he says, "what you were and what I made you, what loveliness I granted you, how great a beauty I bestowed on you. Keep it unharmed for me to the end. For whenever I come to you, I examine your limbs and inquire carefully whether any harm has come to them." The bridegroom says this to those women as well, urging the bride to keep her beauty. 7–8. "There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number. One is my dove, my perfect one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her. Daughters saw her and will call her blessed; queens and concubines too will praise her." We have been taught that there are many different ranks among the godly. The Lord taught this when he said: "There are many dwelling places with my Father." And in the distribution of the talents, not everyone received five talents. One received five, another two, another one, each according to his ability. And in the parable of the sowing he says: "Other seed fell on the good ground and bore fruit, thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold." He calls all of it good ground, not only the ground that yielded a hundred, but also the ground that yielded sixty and thirty. Thirty is a number of the praised, for it has three tens united by the Triad. Sixty has a double blessing, since thirty doubled produces sixty. A hundred is the most perfect: it leaves the left hand and begins on the right, and it is completed in ten tens. Those skilled in such matters call it a square. Yet although the hundred is perfect, the sixty and the thirty are also among the praised, for the Lord called all of it good ground. Let us understand, then, that the bride is the souls perfected in all philosophy and virtue. These souls endure the labors of virtue only out of love for the bridegroom, and they choose to do and suffer everything. Blessed Paul was such a one when he said: "For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God which

is in Christ Jesus our Lord." By these words he teaches us that he does not long for Christ for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Rather, he would choose to lose the kingdom and fall into Gehenna while loving Christ, sooner than reign deprived of that love. Souls like these, held by longing for the bridegroom alone, make up the company of the bride. There are others who are like hired laborers: they put up with the sweat of virtue out of desire for the good things to come. I think these are the ones here called queens, since they desire the kingdom and choose to bear the labors of piety for its sake. There are still others who have not yet been granted freedom but are still willing to be slaves, and who fulfill the divine laws out of fear of Gehenna. I take these to be the ones called concubines, for the bridegroom keeps company with such people too, becoming all things to all. And there are others who live in sloth. They are neither held by love for the bridegroom, nor drawn by longing for the kingdom, nor spurred by fear of Gehenna, and they manage their own affairs rather carelessly. They hold their faith unshaken, keep the doctrines of piety intact, and turn away from all heretical and foreign teaching. Yet they live carelessly: at times they take care of themselves, at times they roll back into sloth; at times they sin, at times they pour out tears of repentance. These the bridegroom here calls maidens. And since such people outnumber both the queens and the concubines, he says: "and maidens without number." They cannot be counted, he means, not only because of their multitude but also because they are unworthy of being numbered. For of the worthy, even the hairs are numbered by the Father. Yet the bridegroom sometimes keeps company even with these, wishing to draw them away from their sloth, leading them toward perfection and working for their salvation in every way. Let us ask why he spoke of sixty queens and eighty concubines. The number sixty has six tens. Ten signifies perfection, and six is the number of the making of the world, for in six days the God of all fashioned the whole creation. So he named sixty queens the souls perfected in virtue in this world who desire the kingdom. The bride lives as a citizen above this world. She is outside it and flies above it, she belongs wholly to the bridegroom, and she pictures him continually. These others live as citizens in this world and pursue the perfection of virtue as far as they can, aiming to obtain the kingdom. Those who fulfill the laws out of fear of judgment are fittingly called eighty. For

divine Scripture calls the time of judgment "the eighth." Blessed David, when he spoke of the judgment in the Psalms, gave the psalm the title "For the eighth," and at the beginning he says: "Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath." And a little later: "For in death there is no one who remembers you, and in Hades who will confess you?" He is teaching that at the time of judgment no room for repentance will be given to those who sinned and did not repent. Since these people followed the divine laws out of fear of these things, not out of longing for the kingdom or love for the bridegroom, they are fittingly said to be eighty: the number eight signifies the eighth, and ten signifies perfection. But he says the bride is better than both the sixty and the eighty: "For one is my dove, my perfect one." Once again he calls her spiritual, and one. Above the sixty and the eighty, she is the only one of her mother. Her mother is the holy font, the Jerusalem above. "And she is the chosen one of her who bore her." The others too were born of her, but this one she has honored above them all and holds as her chosen daughter. Therefore "daughters saw her and will call her blessed," that is, the maidens. And not only they, but queens and concubines too will praise her. For she has surpassed them all, since she pursues the highest philosophy not for reward, nor from fear of punishment, but out of longing for the bridegroom. May we, helped by divine grace, attain the perfection of the bride. If we are too weak for that, may we at least be among the queens. If we fall short even of these, may we not be far from the concubines. And if we prove unworthy even of these, may we at least be enrolled among the maidens, keep the confession of piety untouched, and not be wholly deprived of fellowship with the bridegroom, but enjoy his loveliness by his grace. For to him be glory to the ages of ages. Amen.

So let us now ask for the meaning of the remaining words of the Song of Songs to be made clear, and let us cry out: "Unveil our eyes, and we will perceive the wonders of your law." For he himself gives a word to those who proclaim the good news with great power. He himself said: "Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it." He often grants his grace even to the unworthy, for the benefit of the many. We are confident, then, that he will now reveal to us the depth of the text as well. He will do so not because we deserve it but for the benefit of those who will read or hear the interpretation. Come, then, let us boldly venture on what remains. 9. "Who is this who looks out like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, awe-inspiring as ordered ranks?" In the preceding verses the bridegroom described the bride's beauty in words. He praised each of her limbs separately and then offered praise of her as a whole. And, as in an encomium composed according to the rules of the art, he also made a comparison: he set the bride beside the maidens, the concubines and the queens, and showed her to be far superior. He said her beauty was so great that even those compared with her do not envy her. They admit defeat and call her blessed and thrice-blessed. Here, the bridegroom's attendants have been taught by him about the bride's beauty, her good order and her grace, and urged to come to know her more closely. Out of their great delight they cry out (for her beauty of soul was still hidden under the veil of the body): "Who is this who looks out like the dawn?" Until then her light was seen only in part, veiled by this corruptible body. The dawn is the boundary between night and day: it announces the beginning of the one and the end of the other, and signals that day is coming. In the same way, in the present life, the souls perfected in piety and in all wisdom, which divine Scripture calls the Church and the bride, send out brief gleams of their own virtue. "But when," as blessed Paul says, "this corruptible body puts on incorruption, and this mortal body puts on immortal[ity]

[?] gibbous, but a perfect full moon, lacking nothing and showing its whole circle lit up. That is how she is "beautiful," he says, "as a chosen moon." Those skilled in these matters say that the moon receives its light from the sun's rays. It takes little light when only a small part of it faces the sun. But when it stands directly opposite and sees the whole sun, it takes the imprint of the whole disc like a mirror, is lit up entirely, and leaves no part of its body unlit. So it is with the Church of Christ, the assembly of souls perfected in virtue. As blessed Paul says, "with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror," it "is being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Lord, the Spirit." It becomes wholly full of light, so that it resembles the moon, and a chosen moon, that is, a full one. And it resembles not only the moon but also the sun, a sun that fills those who see it with awe. I do not think this phrase was placed here idly, for nothing is said at random by the divine Spirit. Life is night, as blessed Paul says: "The night is far spent, the day is at hand." So, as in the night, the Church is necessarily like a moon, giving light to travelers and showing them the straight road. She is also like the dawn, since the time after the Lord's coming is like a dawn: it signals the state to come as the coming of a day. "For we shall find him ready like the dawn," it says. But when the great and glorious day of the Lord arrives, in the prophet's words, the day of which blessed Paul says, "The day is at hand," then she will no longer shine like the moon. She will shine like the sun, filling with awe not only unbelieving people but also the maidens, the concubines, the queens, and the bodiless powers themselves. The Lord himself is witness to this when he says: "Then the righteous will shine like the sun." And blessed Paul says: "There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory." So the bride of Christ looks out like the dawn, for at present her beauty is known only in part. "And she is beautiful as a chosen moon," filled with the Lord's light and illuminating the world with her rays. That is why the Lord in the holy Gospels said to his holy disciples: "You are the light of the world." And to show what kind of light, he adds: "So let your light shine before people, that, knowing your good works, they may glorify your Father in heaven." She is not only [beautiful]

as a chosen moon. In the life to come she will also blaze like the sun, astonishing everyone with her radiance. They will marvel not only at her light but also at her order. For in the Lord's bride nothing is disordered, nothing undefined, nothing confused. As if by a plumb line she sets straight what must be done, and with rule and square she orders her own life. After the praises of the bridegroom's attendants, the bride, telling of her own affairs, says: 10–11. "I went down into the nut garden to look among the produce of the torrent, to see whether the vine had flowered, whether the pomegranates had blossomed. There I will give you my breasts. My soul did not know; it made me the chariots of Aminadab." The meaning is buried deep under the obscurity of the words. But let us call on divine grace for help, dig down into the depth, and bring up the treasure. The assembly of the godly, which divine Scripture calls the bride, teaches that the godly are not content with their own salvation. They do not think it enough to obtain the hoped-for marriage alone. They put all their zeal into freeing all other people from barrenness, making them fruitful and bringing forth the fruit of virtue. And it teaches that in doing this and offering teaching to others they fell among the chariots of Aminadab, or, as Symmachus translated, "the chariots of the leading people," or, as Aquila has it, "the chariots of the people of a willing ruler." By the nut garden they mean the present life, which is bitter, hard and toilsome, but holds the fruit of virtue hidden within it. For the fruit of the nut has a bitter outer husk, and beneath it a second layer that is hard and resistant. The edible part is stored away as if in an inner chamber, hidden, and cannot be got out without effort. The present life is like this. It has bitter pains and griefs, labors and sweat, yet these are not sterile or fruitless; they hold their fruit hidden. That is why blessed Paul says: "Our life is hidden with Christ in God; but when Christ our life is revealed, then we too shall live in him." "So I went down into the nut garden," that is, into human life. And why did you go down, O bride? "To look among the produce of the torrent." Here again she calls the things of this present life a torrent. A torrent does not flow all year round: it runs in winter, but in summer it stops and dries up. Such are the pleasures of life. At present glory, wealth, kingship, luxury and the other flowers of life rush along like a torrent. But when the life to come appears, they wane and cease, and

…ceases, like a winter torrent. “I went down, then,” she says, “into the garden of nuts, to look at the produce of the torrent,” wanting to learn “whether the pomegranates had blossomed.” In life, some people are figuratively called vines and others pomegranates, according to their different achievements in virtue. Some bear love and cherish concord, joined together in mind like the seeds of a pomegranate. Others cultivate wine worthy of the Father’s winepresses, because they have been eager to give themselves to contemplation. By “going down” she means condescension. Blessed Paul too became weak to the weak, so that he might win the weak, and to those without the law he became like one without the law, though he was not without law toward God but under the law of Christ, so that he might win those without the law. “I went down, then,” she says, “into the garden of nuts,” taking care of the produce of the torrent and the fruits of the vine and the pomegranate. I will not keep away from you, not even there: “I will give you my breasts,” that is, the streams of my teaching. For you take as your own what is done to them, and you say, “Whatever you did to one of the least of these little ones, you did to me.” To this she adds: “My soul did not know; it made me chariots of Aminadab.” Symmachus translated this more clearly when he said: “My soul perplexed me because of the chariots of a people’s leader.” “For while I do these things,” she says, “I am perplexed and astonished. I have worked for their salvation, yet they have attacked me. They obey the devil who commands them, become his chariots, as it were, and are driven by him.” For Aminadab is interpreted as “of a people’s leader” or “of a people’s ruler.” One can understand this precisely from Aquila, from Symmachus and from the fifth version. So the bride, that is, the choir of those made perfect in virtue, says: We take every care for the unbelievers and contrive in every way to obtain salvation for them. But some of them have become chariots, as it were, of the ruler of this age, who now works in the sons of disobedience, as blessed Paul says, and they have attacked me, repaying good with evil. One can clearly find this both in the Acts of the Apostles and in the letters of blessed Paul. When the apostles preached the word of godliness, they persuaded some to believe, but the unbelievers drove them out and abused them. They were tortured on the rack and endured countless kinds of death. Blessed Paul is witness to this when he says: “In labors more abundantly, in beatings beyond measure, in prisons more abundantly, in deaths often. Five times I received forty lashes less one; three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I have spent in the deep; in journeys often,

in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers,” and so on. When the bride has said these things, the bridegroom’s attendants answer her and say: “Return, return, O Shulammite; return, return, and we will look upon you.” Aquila translated this more clearly: “Return,” he says, “return, you who are at peace.” This book calls our Lord Solomon, the peaceable one. In the same way it calls his bride “at peace,” because she has received peace from him and been freed from the earlier war. The bridegroom’s attendants see her driven and attacked by those chariots, so they encourage her and say: “Return, you who are at peace; return, return, and we will look upon you.” This means: do not fear your persecutors, but hold fast to the teaching and bring out the proclamation of the teaching. Do not dread the chariots and do not fear war, since you are called “at peace.” If you keep on preaching, we will see your kingdom. The Lord’s words to blessed Paul are like this. Paul too grew weary and was distressed by his many trials, and he says: “A thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to buffet me, so that I would not be too elated. Three times I begged the Lord about this, that it might leave me.” The Lord answers him: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” The bridegroom’s attendants say the same thing here: “Return, return, O Shulammite; return, return, and we will look upon you.” The bridegroom then says to them:

CHAPTER 7. 1. “What will you see in the Shulammite, who comes like dances of the camps?” He means: What do you expect to see in her who is at peace? Do not hope to behold some cheap or partial goods, for look, she “comes like dances of the camps.” The two words seem somehow opposed to each other, since dances do not go with camps. Dances belong to festivals and camps belong to soldiers, and war is the opposite of a festival. But this bride is made up of [?] holy ones. She resembles camps because of her courageous and noble spirit and her soldier’s full armor, and she is a dance because she carries divine hymns in her mouth. Blessed David shows the first of these when he says: “The sound of rejoicing and salvation is in the tents of the righteous.” And again: “Appoint

a feast with leafy branches, up to the horns of the altar.” Blessed Paul points to the camps when he says: “For the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly but powerful through God for tearing down strongholds. We tear down arguments and every lofty thing raised up against the knowledge of God, and we take every thought captive to obey Christ.” And again: “Take up the full armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day, and having done everything, to stand firm.” Like a general, he also supplies the soldiers with their weapons, saying: “Stand, then, with your waist girded with truth, wearing the breastplate of righteousness, and with your feet shod with the readiness of the gospel of peace. Above all, take up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the flaming arrows of the evil one. Receive the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” To learn that they resemble not only camps but also dances, let us hear the Lord saying: “Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom.” So the bridegroom rightly says: “What will you see in the Shulammite, who comes like dances of the camps?” He did not say “the camps of the dances” but “the dances of the camps.” For the dances come out of the camps. The athletes of virtue win their victories in the camps, then return singing songs of triumph and dance as they sing the victory hymn. Having said this to the attendants, the bridegroom turns his speech to the bride and says: “How beautiful your steps have become in sandals, O daughter of Nadab!” Aquila has “of a ruler” and Symmachus “of a leader.” Who else could this leader or ruler be but the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit? He also says to her in Psalm 44: “Listen, daughter, and incline your ear. Forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty, for he is your Lord.” Blessed David teaches that the Holy Spirit also bears the title of leader when he says: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a leading Spirit.” So the bridegroom praises the bride’s steps, because they are straight and travel the royal road, and because they shine finely in their sandals. Blessed Paul taught what the sandals are when he said: “With your feet shod with the readiness of the gospel of peace.” The beauty of these feet (Ps. [?]; Eph. 6:15; Isa. 52:7)

was foreseen by the prophet Isaiah, who said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of peace, of those who bring good news of good things!” The bridegroom uses the same words in this book when he says: “How beautiful your steps have become, O daughter of Nadab!” But we should draw some contemplation not only from the interpretation of the name but also from the name itself, so let us ask who Nadab was. He was a son of Aaron. He brought strange fire into the tabernacle of God and met the end of his life. In the same way we find the Lord’s bride, I mean the Church, bringing into the divine tabernacle not the fire of the law but the new fire. She received this fire from the bridegroom himself: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled!” Having brought this new fire into the divine tabernacle through the New Covenant, she cries out: “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.” So he rightly calls her “daughter of Nadab,” since she has used the new fire to offer human beings as a whole burnt offering. They differ in their intention in changing the fire, but he and she performed one and the same act. We have said this for the present so as not to leave even the name without contemplation. The bridegroom again goes through her members one by one, offers each of them fitting praise, and says: “The curves of your thighs are like necklaces, the work of a craftsman’s hands. (2, 5.) Your navel is a turned bowl that never lacks mixed wine. Your belly is a heap of wheat fenced in with lilies. Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle. Your neck is like a tower of ivory. Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, at the gates of the daughter of many. Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, looking toward Damascus. Your head upon you is like Carmel, and the braid of your head is like purple. A king is bound in the galleries.” Earlier the bridegroom began from her upper parts when he praised her. Now he begins from the steps and sandals and has gone up to the braid of her head. After the sandals and steps he admires not the thighs themselves but the curves of the thighs, and he says they resemble necklaces made by a craftsman. He means this: in those necklaces the stones are set into the gold with perfect harmony, so that onlookers admire not only the materials, the gold and the stones, but also the goldsmith’s art. In the same way, each part of practical virtue is adorned with proportion and harmony. He figuratively called practical virtue thighs, because by means of them we make our way and do

what we wish. So the bridegroom begins from the practical when he admires the bride, and goes up to contemplation. At the beginning he did the opposite: he started from contemplation and came to practice, for he said, “Your eyes are doves,” and by this he signified the spiritual quality of the soul’s power of sight. Here he admires practical virtue first, and quite rightly. First we are enlightened: we open the closed eyes of the soul, receive the divine light and are confirmed in faith. Only then do we proceed to practical virtue. For this reason, when the bridegroom wove his first song of praise, he began from the eyes, which were the first to receive healing. But now that the bride’s beauty has become perfect, he begins from below, from practical virtue, and goes up to contemplation as he praises the bride’s loveliness. First he praises the steps and the sandals, then the curves of the thighs, that is, each of the deeds done. After the thighs comes the navel: “Your navel,” he says, “is a turned bowl that never lacks mixed wine.” If you please, let us set beside this what the God of all said about the navel of Judea through the prophet Ezekiel. He was exposing her licentiousness and making her great impiety public, as we explained in the first discourse, and he says to the prophet: “Testify to Jerusalem of her iniquities and say: Thus says the Lord to Jerusalem: Your root and your birth are from the land of Canaan. Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite. As for your birth, on the day you were born your navel was not cut.” To that woman he says, “Your navel was not cut,” but to this one, “Your navel is a turned bowl that never lacks mixed wine.” The one born from Egypt did not cut her navel. Instead she drew the wickedness of impious teaching out of Egypt, as though through a root. This one did not merely cut her navel. She made the cut so deep that she tore out the whole root of idolatry. So she is compared to a turned bowl: she always has the mixed wine of godliness, and the delight that godliness produces in her never fails. Further: “Your belly is a heap of wheat fenced in with lilies.” This means: the storerooms of your soul are full of hidden mysteries, and only their fragrance is known to those who are still imperfect and infants. “For it is fenced in,” he says, “with lilies.” By the fence we are to understand what is hidden, and by the lilies the fragrance that flows out from there in every direction. “And your two breasts are like twin fawns of a gazelle.” For the streams of your teaching pour out new waters and teach keenness of sight and spiritual contemplation. For the gazelle (dorkas)

takes its name from keen sight (oxydorkia), and the fawn (nebros) signifies what is new (neos). “And your neck is like a tower of ivory.” For it has stopped being black and has been made white by taking on my yoke. To enemies it is fearsome like a tower, and to friends it is lovely because it shines. “And your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, at the gates of the daughter of many.” When Aquila translated this, he put “reckoning” in place of “Heshbon.” So the bridegroom teaches that the eyes of pious souls are pools that receive the divine streams and are always overflowing, since they take in the streams from many gates, that is, from many mouths. He figuratively called the mouths gates. For they receive the streams of benefit from the great Moses, from Joshua the son of Nun, from Samuel the prophet, from David the prophet and king, from Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel and Ezekiel, from the twelve prophets, from the divine Gospels, from the holy apostles and from the teachers who came after them. That is why the bridegroom says: “Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, at the gates of the daughter of many.” He means: The contemplations of your soul and the multitude of your pious thoughts are like pools that receive water from many sides, since you receive the streams of teaching from many mouths. “And your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, looking toward Damascus.” Because Judea was disobedient and unruly, her nose received a ring as a kind of bridle, as a goring bull does, and that ring was the threat of the law, since “Israel ran wild like a frenzied heifer.” But the bride’s “nose,” he says, “is like the tower of Lebanon, looking toward Damascus.” For it is high and lifted up. It perceives the fragrance from above, holds fast to the bridegroom’s perfume and cries out: “We will run after you toward the scent of your perfumes.” That is why it is likened to a tower that stands on Lebanon and looks toward Damascus. According to blessed Paul, the devil disguises himself as an angel of light, and he also passes himself off as a spiritual perfume. So the bride’s nose must stay awake and sober and keep watch toward Damascus, so that she is not deceived into abandoning the true perfume and following the false and misleading one. Divine Scripture often uses Damascus to stand for the Gentiles and for the impiety that ruled at that time. Blessed Isaiah, for example, prophesied the Lord’s birth and said in the person of the Spirit: “I went in to the prophetess,” that is, to the virgin, “and she conceived in her womb and bore a son.” He goes on to say: “And the

Lord said to me: Call his name, Plunder Quickly, Despoil Swiftly. For before the child knows how to say ‘father’ or ‘mother,’ he will take the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria before the king of the Assyrians.” This shows that while he is still a child he will overthrow the one figuratively called the king of the Assyrians, that is, the devil. He will take over the power of Damascus, that is, the might of idolatry, and he himself will become master of those whom the devil had taken captive. “For he will take,” it says, “the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria.” He freed both those from the Jews and those from the Gentiles, delivered them from error, overthrew the tyrant and made them his own. So he rightly says to the bride: “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, looking toward Damascus.” For you keep watch all around, so that the devil does not imitate divine things and deceive you by setting falsehood in battle against the truth. “And your head,” he says, “is like Carmel,” that is, filled with every good thing. For the God of all says this through the prophet when he rebukes the ingratitude of the Jews: “And I brought you into Carmel, to eat its fruit and its good things.” He means: Your head is like Carmel, which produces every kind of good thing and bears every fruit for me, the farmer. Then comes: “And the braid of your head is like purple; a king is bound in the galleries.” Your hair was once loose, and for that reason it was likened to the flocks of goats that appeared in Gilead. Now it has been braided. Not only has it been braided, it has also taken on a marvelous dye, and it is like a king clothed in purple who runs about everywhere. By a braid of hair likened to royal purple he means teaching that is presented with harmony and adorned, as with flowers, with the blood of Christ. A king clothed in purple does not shine as brightly as the teacher of godliness who weaves the proclamation of the knowledge of God and presents it to those nurtured by the truth. (6, 7.) “How beautiful you have become, and how sweet, O love, in your delights! Your stature is like the palm tree, and your breasts like the clusters.” He means: You have become beautiful, though you were not beautiful before. You were full of everything unpleasant, and suddenly you have appeared sweet. You obtained these things by delighting in love: you loved the bridegroom who loved you, counted your affection for him a delight, and despised everything else. That is why “you have become beautiful and sweet, and your stature is like the palm tree, and your breasts like the clusters.” For you have not only beauty but also height, likened to a palm tree. “And your breasts are like its clusters.” For being [?] and

…lofty, reaching to the vaults of heaven, you still stoop down to the weak and hold out your breasts, the nipples of your teaching, to those who need teaching. A palm tree, after all, has its clusters hanging downward. The Holy Spirit says this through blessed David as well: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree.” So the bride hears these praises. The many words of acclaim give her wings, and love sets her on fire, and she says: 8–9. I said, I will go up to the palm tree, I will take hold of its heights; and your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine, and the scent of your nostril like apples, and your throat like good wine, going to my beloved for uprightness, sufficing for my lips and teeth. From this we can learn exactly how the bride longs for the bridegroom. She yearns for the ascent and pictures the height to herself. As blessed Paul says, she “does not consider that she has attained, but presses on to lay hold of it; forgetting what lies behind, she strains forward to what lies ahead.” We must ask how the bridegroom can be both a palm and a vine, bearing no palm fruit but producing clusters of the vine. Aquila's version will guide us to the hidden meaning. Where we have “I will take hold of its heights,” he has “I will take hold of its spathes.” Spathes are the fruit of male palm trees, and when they are placed on the female palms they make the fruit of those trees hold fast and ripen. So the bride is eager to receive from the bridegroom the seeds of pious thoughts, and she says: “I said, I will go up to the palm tree and take hold of its heights,” or, as Aquila has it, “its spathes.” “And your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine.” For you are the true vine. The saving wine is cultivated from you and pressed out in the spiritual winepresses, and from these the cup is filled that makes one drunk as with the very best wine. “And the scent of your nostril is like the fragrance of the apple.” The very organ with which you smell gives off to me a fragrance like that of apples. What we said about apples at the beginning of the book is enough on that subject. “And your throat like good wine going to my beloved for uprightness, sufficing for my lips and teeth.” The teaching that comes from your throat is better than any fragrant wine and any delight in life. You offer it, my beloved, because you wish to set straight the souls that have believed in you. It is enough and more than enough for me: some of it I bring out and proclaim, using my lips as instruments, while the rest I guard and keep, setting my teeth in place of [Apparatus: “therefore” is missing from the codex; for “and” the codex has “but.”]

a wall in front of it. This agrees with what blessed Paul said: “For I heard,” he says, “inexpressible words, which no human being is permitted to speak.” That is why the bride too says, “sufficing for my lips and my teeth”: some things I bring out, others I keep. To this she adds: 10. I am my beloved's, and his turning is toward me. I have dedicated myself to him and shunned all foreign fellowship, whether Greek, Jewish or heretical. He in turn has preferred me to all others, and his turning is toward me. Once he had nowhere to lay his head, but now he has found a place to lay his head. Though he has many concubines, queens and maidens, he prefers me to them all. Yet I cannot bear to enjoy his holy fellowship alone. 11–13. Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field and lodge in the villages. Let us rise early and go to the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has blossomed, whether the blossom has opened, whether the pomegranates have blossomed. There I will give you my breasts. The mandrakes have given forth their scent, and at our doors are all kinds of fruit, new as well as old; what my mother gave me, my beloved, I have kept for you. The bride urges the bridegroom to care also for humble, lowly souls, which she calls by figure “field” and “villages” because they are lowly and small. She does not say, “Let us go out to the city,” but “Let us go out into the field, let us lodge in the villages, let us rise early and go to the vineyards, let us see whether the vine has blossomed.” Let us visit, she means, those who have just received the preaching. “Whether the blossom has opened”: let us look also at those who are further along, who have put forth not only leaves but the flower itself, which she here calls the “blossom.” “Whether the pomegranates have blossomed”: whether, she means, a beginning of love has appeared in some of them. We must go round about and give them all fitting care, for by doing this I will serve you. “There,” she says, “I will give you my breasts.” For you take as done to yourself what is done to them, and you say: “Whatever you did to one of the least of these little ones, you did to me.” “The mandrakes have given forth their scent.” The mandrake is known to cause sleep, as the physicians say. We have been commanded to “put to death the members that are on earth.” This does not mean handing the members themselves over to death, but making them dead to evil deeds. So she fittingly puts the mandrake here and says, “The mandrakes have given forth their scent,” meaning that people have begun to sleep to their sins. Just as those who have drunk mandrake do not feel the movements of the body, so those who drain the cup of pious teaching are eager to lull the passions (Matt. 18 [?]:40; Col. 3:5)

to sleep. And it is not only that the mandrakes have given forth their scent; “at our doors are all kinds of fruit” as well. Those who have received our teaching bear fruit of every kind. “And new as well as old, what my mother gave me, I have kept for you, my beloved.” I received the commandments of the Old Testament and the counsels of the New from my mother, the grace of the Spirit, and I have kept them for you. I have guarded the deposit unharmed. Like this are the words blessed Paul wrote to Timothy: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day.” Like it too is what the Lord said in the Gospel: “Every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a man who brings out of his treasure things new and old.”

CHAPTER 8. 1–2. Who will grant you to me, my beloved, nursing at my mother's breasts? Finding you outside, I will kiss you, and no one will despise me. I will take you and bring you into my mother's house, into the chamber of her who conceived me. You will teach me; I will give you spiced wine to drink, and the juice of my pomegranates. In his humanity he too received the whole grace of the Spirit. “For the child Jesus,” Scripture says, “grew and became strong in the Spirit, and the grace of God was upon him.” So the bride, astonished at his inexpressible love for humankind, says: “You too nursed at my mother's breasts.” To keep both the sequence and the harmony of the words, let us start a little further back and go through the meaning in summary. She is saying: “I received from my mother not only new things but old ones too, and I will keep them for you. And you, out of your great love for humankind, took on my nature yourself and were willing to nurse at the same breasts as I, so that in this too you might show that we are kin. You nursed not because you needed to, but to teach me how I ought to nurse and from what breast I should draw grace. That is why you came to baptism. It was not to wash away the filth of sins, for you committed no sin, and no deceit was found in your mouth. Nor was it to receive the

[?] I say: “Who will grant you to me, my beloved, nursing at my mother's breasts?” Drawn by this love of yours for humankind, “finding you outside, I will kiss you, and no one will despise me; I will take you and bring you into my mother's house, into the chamber of her who conceived me; I will give you spiced wine to drink, and the juice of my pomegranates.” I am drunk with love for you, so I will embrace and kiss you wherever I find you, not only in the bedchamber and the bridal room but also in the marketplace and in public. Those who see me do this will not [?] blame me, since they know the flame of love. Then I will take you from there and “bring you into my mother's house, into the chamber of her who conceived me.” What is the house of the all-holy Spirit (for it was the Spirit that gave birth to the bride), if not the divine temple, which imitates the Jerusalem above? Those who enter there speak with the bridegroom boldly, since they have received the dignity of the bride. “And there,” she says, “I will give you spiced wine to drink, and the juice of my pomegranates.” By “spiced wine” she means teaching that is seasoned with divine grace, perfumed, as it were, and fragrant. By “the juice of pomegranates” she means the benefit that comes from the fruits of love. 3. After saying this to the bridegroom, the bride also speaks to the maidens and says: His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me. For I am above the threat of punishment, and I gather the blessings of your right hand. That is why his left hand

4. I have put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and by the strengths of the field, that you rouse and awaken love until it pleases. You must keep it constantly burning and stir it up, so that you may long for him ardently and reach perfection as he wishes. 5. When she has said this, [the maidens], seeing how she surpasses all, are amazed and say: [?] leaning on her beloved? They do not say “white” but “made white,” for she was black. Of the bridegroom the bride says, “My beloved is white,” not “made white,” for he was white by nature. She, however, had been darkened (for the sun had looked askance at her), and was then made white and given a share in the bridegroom's whiteness. He is light, and he made her light and called her so; he is holy, and he made her holy; he became the resurrection, and he counted her worthy of resurrection. In the same way he gave her a share in his own whiteness as well. That is why

the maidens who see her say: “Who is this who comes up made white, leaning on her beloved?” For he guides her steps and, as it were, leads her by the hand, and through her firm faith in him she makes the ascent and journey into the heavens to the one she loves. After this the bridegroom speaks and says: “Under the apple tree I roused you; there your mother was in labor with you, there she who bore you was in labor with you.” We will understand these words if we recall what the bride said at the beginning of the book. She said to the bridegroom: “As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons; I longed for his shade and sat in it, and his fruit was sweet to my throat.” The things given to us in the present are the shadow of the good things to come (“For now,” says blessed Paul, “I see as in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face”). The bride longed to sit in the shade of the bridegroom, that is, in the pledge given to us now (she called him an apple tree for the reasons we have given). So the bridegroom has good reason to say: “Under the apple tree I roused you; there she who bore you was in labor with you.” For we believed the preaching about our Savior and came to divine baptism, and when we came we obtained new birth. It was the grace of the Spirit that was in labor with us, and the history of the Acts bears witness to this. When the most divine Peter had addressed the crowd and set before those who had gathered the preaching about the Savior, the writer says that when they heard the word they were cut to the heart and said to Peter: “What shall we do to be saved?” He said to them: “Believe, and let each of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and you will receive the promise of the Holy Spirit.” Fittingly, then, the bridegroom says to the bride: “Under the apple tree I roused you; there your mother was in labor with you; there she who bore you was in labor with you.” The repetition is not there without reason: he wanted to show who the mother is, and so he called the birth to mind. After this he urges her, saying: 6. Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm; for love is strong as death, jealousy is hard as Hades; its sparks are sparks of fire, coals of fire are its flames. Some copies, in place of “coals of fire, its sparks, sparks of fire,” have “its wings are wings, coals of fire are its flames.” So the bridegroom says to pious souls, which divine Scripture calls the bride: “Set me as a seal in your heart and on your arm.” By “heart” he means the contemplative part of the soul,

and by “arm” the active part. That is why the right shoulder and the breast were set apart from the people for the priests. So our Savior wants us to have him as our seal when we speak and when we think, and to stamp with his image both what we say and what we do. In this way we will be royal coins, not counterfeit, but bearing the king's image. And this, he says, is easy for you to do if you gain love for me. “For it is strong as death.” Just as death, after the divine sentence, prevailed over everyone, so love prevails over everything and is stronger even than death itself. Gain jealousy as well. If you gain it too, you will not bear to see another soul honored above you, with you lacking boldness while she enjoys fellowship with me. “For jealousy is hard,” and as hard to overcome as Hades. He named Hades according to the common opinion, giving death this name as well. So strong is love that [?] it has wings, and about its wings it has a flame of fire and sends out sparks. What could be [?] than love that burns like this? And its fire is not the kind that can be put out. 7. For much water, he says, cannot quench love, and rivers will not sweep it away. All the saints who stood out in the Old Testament and in the New bear witness to this. Abraham's love for God was not quenched by his life in a foreign land, or the pressure of famine, or the seizing of his wife, or the offering of his son, or the quarrel over the wells. Isaac's love was not quenched by the sorrows that befell him, nor Jacob's by his constant toils and lifelong griefs. What was harsher than Joseph's trials? He was sold by his brothers and robbed of a loving mother and father, of his ancestral home, his freedom and his wealth. He served as a slave though he did not deserve it, fell victim to slander because of his chastity, was sent to prison, and endured countless terrible things. Yet his love for God proved stronger than all of them. What need is there to speak of the great Moses, of Joshua the general, and of the great prophets Samuel, David, Elijah and Elisha? What was more frenzied than the Babylonians? What was more fearsome than the furnace they lit? Yet even that furnace did not quench the flame of love in those three youths; rather, it kindled it and stirred it up. What was more terrifying than those lions to which the great Daniel was handed over? Yet his love for God made him too more powerful than they. And

to set aside the other saints for now, blessed Paul alone is enough to teach us love's strength, since he above all others had experienced it. “Who will separate us,” he says, “from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? As it is written, For your sake we are being killed all day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter. But in all these things,” he says, “we are more than conquerors through Christ who loved us.” These words are enough to show love's victory, but what comes next proclaims it still more clearly. He goes on: “For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.” To show that love is more powerful than all things, both visible and invisible, he fashions in words a creature that does not exist, sets it against love as well, and shows that love for God is stronger even than that. Fittingly, then, the bridegroom says: “Much water cannot quench love, and rivers will not sweep it away. If a man gives all his living for love, they will utterly despise him.” It is those deprived and stripped of love who despise the one who gives all his living for love. That is why blessed Paul said: “When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we appeal; we have become like the refuse of the world, the scum of all things, to this very day.” This is truly what happens to people who are dizzy: they are the ones who cannot stand steady, yet they think everything around them is spinning. In the same way, those deprived of love abused love's nurslings as senseless fools. Yet even this did love no harm; it only made love warmer. When reviled, the apostles blessed; when slandered, they appealed; and having become, as it were, the refuse of the world, they said they were the scum of all things to this very day. 8–9. Our sister is little, and she has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day she is spoken for? If she is a wall, let us build silver battlements upon her; if she is a door, let us carve a cedar panel upon her. I think it is the holy prophets, who stood out in the Old Testament, who say this among themselves. They see how small the bride's spiritual stature is and how her breasts are still undeveloped and hidden, and as matchmakers and heralds of the marriage they say: “The king is about

to take the bride, our sister, but she is small and has no breasts. She is not yet fruitful; she cannot yet supply the milk of teaching or offer solid food to those who need it. So we must consider what to do. She is about to be united to the great King and to be, as it were, the wall of his house, keeping and guarding what is inside, and to serve as a door that protects what is stored within. So let us build on her, as on a wall, ‘silver battlements’, that is, battlements of reason that shine with speech. ‘For the words of the Lord are pure words, silver refined by fire, tested in the earth.’ Standing on them she can strike her enemies and pursue those who plot against her. And as on a door, let us fix on her panels made of cedar, which do not let in the rot of sin, for cedar does not rot.” The bride, trusting in the bridegroom's generosity and riches, answers them: 10. I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers. In his eyes I was as one who finds peace. He foreknew me and predestined me. He knew that I would seek peace and pursue it, and that in pursuing it I would attain it. So he called me peaceful, and the Shulammite, and made me an unbreakable wall that strikes fear into the enemy. And my breasts, that is, my moral and theological teaching, he raised on high and made like a tower, so that from there I might make war on the bridegroom's enemies and destroy them. Not only am I a wall, as I said, but

11. For Solomon, she says, had a vineyard in Baal-hamon. He gave his vineyard to keepers; each man will bring a thousand pieces of silver for its fruit. Symmachus rendered “in Baal-hamon” as “in the possession of a people,” and Aquila as “in one that has a multitude.” Long ago God entrusted this vineyard to Israel. But they not only stoned and killed the servants sent to collect the fruit; they even crucified the heir himself. So, as the Master said, the vineyard was taken from them and given to a nation that produces its fruit. That is why the bride says that “Solomon,” that is, the peaceful one, “had a vineyard in Baal-hamon,” that is, in the possession of a people, or in one that has a multitude, and “he gave it to keepers.” By the vineyard she means the people who have come to piety. The keepers, who tend and guard it, are those honored with the priesthood, who are charged with providing both the watering of spiritual teaching and protection. And she says: “Each man will bring a thousand pieces of silver for its fruit.” The number signifies

…the unit of the right hand. This signifies the salvation of the one who bears fruit, for the one who planted the vineyard receives no other fruit from it than the salvation of the very one who was planted and bears fruit. That is why the bride says this: (12) "My vineyard, my own, is before me; the thousand are for Solomon." What she means is this (for what is obscure must be made as clear as possible): "The vineyard is mine," she says, "and the fruit is mine. The thousand pieces of silver that seem to be paid to my peaceable bridegroom, that is, to Solomon, are before me, for he will give them back to me. Even now he demands fruit because he longs for my salvation, and he wants to see me saved." "My vineyard, my own, is before me; the thousand are for Solomon, and the two hundred for those who keep its fruit." The keepers receive a wage for the vineyard, and a fixed wage. Since they guard the five senses of the vineyard, sight, taste, smell, hearing and touch, they rightly receive the two hundred, which is a fifth of the thousand. For those who guard the divine vineyard deserve to receive recompense from the one who planted it. Therefore not only the bridegroom but also the bride herself will give them their rewards. Blessed Paul too says: "If anyone's work that he has built on it remains, he will receive a reward." And when evening came, the master of the house ordered that those who had worked in the vineyard be given a denarius each. It is clear, then, that nothing goes unrewarded with God. For if the one who offers a cup of cold water to one of the least of the little ones will not lose his reward, much more will the one who guards the vineyard enjoy the recompense that comes from the vineyard. The vineyard itself will offer obedience through the five senses and will make up the two hundred, which, taken five times over, [?] are apportioned to those who actually guard them. For the number one thousand shows the perfection that is in Christ. It is a unit lacking nothing, since it contains within itself the principle of the unit not only in potential but also in actuality: it begins from the unit, it is written with the unit, and it produces the unit. For the thousand and the ten thousand are both marked with the letter that stands for one. The number two hundred, in turn, shows the restoration of our nature to itself by keeping the commandments. It multiplies by ten, after the ten commandments, the number made up of four times five, which therefore represents the number twenty, the compound of the matter and form of our nature. In addition to what has been said, the bride, out of deep humility and intense longing for the good things to come, also says the following to the bridegroom:

(13) "You who sit in the gardens, companions are attending; let me hear your voice." This means: "O my bridegroom, you rest in both the intelligible creation and the sensible [?] one, since both were planted like gardens by your will. Besides us there are others who gaze at you without ever turning away, because they are not divided by the bond of the body: these are the immaterial, angelic orders. But I am subject to that bond, and so I fear that I may change. That is why I hasten your second coming and beg you: let me hear that longed-for voice of yours: 'Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you.'" (14) "Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices." For when you call the righteous to your kingdom, prepared for them from the foundation of the world, you entirely withdraw the providence you exercise over us through sensible things. You draw the worthy up to the heights of the spiritual graces, which make them fragrant in a spiritual way through deification. There, like a gazelle or a young stag, which kills venomous beasts, you slay the spirits of wickedness that rage against us, and you end their war against us.
